With devotion, I shall worship with this handful of flower-garlands of my own poem the wondrous deeds of the Sage in his former births— deeds that were glorious, auspicious through their possession of excellent virtues, the abode of fame, and enchanting beyond all reproach.
Since the path to the state of a Sugata is pointed out by these praiseworthy qualities which serve as its distinguishing marks,
even those of harsh minds would surely attain clarity, and discourses on the Dharma would become most delightful.
Having observed that it is for the sake of the world, this effort shall be undertaken by way of a path unimpaired by scripture, the words of the seers, and reasoning,
in order to lead my own intuitive insight to a state of being beloved by the scriptures through the various accounts of the extraordinary deeds of the Supreme Being.

I bow my head to that peerless one, together with his Dharma and Saṅgha, whose splendor of recognized virtues—even by those striving for their own welfare—could never be fully grasped; he whose fame shines with the radiance of infallible words, proclaiming him "the All-Knowing One."
1. The Story of the Tigress:

Since even in his previous births the Blessed One was one whose nature was supremely affectionate toward all beings without cause and who had become the very self of all creatures, one should cultivate the highest faith in the Buddha, the Blessed One.

Thus it is heard that this avadāna of the Blessed One’s former birth is being proclaimed by our own gurus— those who hold the Three Jewels as supreme, who have won over their teachers through the excellence of their practice, and who are preeminent in the accumulation of virtues. It is said that the Bodhisattva, while favoring the world with the outpourings of compassion— such as generosity, pleasant speech, and purposeful conduct, which were consistent with his extraordinary vows and rendered blameless through the mastery of wisdom— he was born into a great, ever-increasing family of pure conduct, devoted to its own dharma.
He took birth within a brahmin family.

Having undergone the sequence of sacramental rites such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) and others, and growing up with natural intelligence, distinguished patronage, curiosity for knowledge, and lack of indolence, he attained in no long time the highest mastery as a teacher in the eighteen branches of learning and in all the arts not contrary to the traditions of his own family.
He was like Brahmā to those who know Brahmā, and like a king to kings, a worthy recipient of great honor;
he was like the thousand-eyed Indra himself to his subjects, acting as a father to those seeking knowledge.
A great abundance of gain, honor, and fame appeared for him, won over by the excellence of his fortune and virtues;

yet the Bodhisattva, whose mind was cultivated through the practice of the Dharma and who was already familiar with the life of renunciation, did not take delight in that. Having purified his intellect through his former conduct, he perceived the multitude of faults inherent in sensual pleasures.
Having cast aside the life of a householder like a state of ill health, he adorned a certain forest retreat.
There, through that detachment, through his tranquility purified by wisdom, and indeed through his very composure,
he seemed to rebuke the world of men, whose peace was shattered by attachment to evil deeds.
With their minds encompassed by a tranquility consisting of loving-kindness that flowed forth from him,
the fierce beasts roamed about like ascetics, their natures turned away from mutual hostility.
Through purity of conduct, restraint of the senses, the practice of contentment, and the quality of compassion,
he became as dear to the people of the world— even those with whom he was unacquainted— as they were to him.
Due to his state of having few desires, being ignorant of hypocrisy, and having abandoned longing for gain, fame, and pleasure,
he inclined even the minds of the deities toward clarity and devotion.

Then, having heard that he had gone forth, men whose hearts were bound by his virtues abandoned their kinsmen and possessions and entered into discipleship under him, as if approaching spiritual perfection itself.
In purity of conduct, in the cultivation of the senses, in the non-forgetfulness of mindfulness, in solitude,
and likewise in the mental concentration of loving-kindness and the rest, he instructed his disciples according to their capacity.
Then once, when that Great Being’s assembly of disciples had mostly reached full maturity,

had expanded, had been established upon this auspicious path, and had been led by him into the true way of renunciation in the world— while the gates to the lower realms were as if closed and the paths to happy rebirths were as if made into royal highways— he was followed by his contemporary disciple Ajita for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life.
He wandered through mountain caves and forest thickets conducive to yoga.
Then, in a mountain cave, he saw a tigress who,
due to the distress of childbirth, had become weak and motionless.
With a pair of eyes sunken from emaciation and a belly exceedingly thinned by hunger,
she looked even upon her own young children as if they were food.

She was scolding with cruel cries of "ro-roo" those who had approached her out of thirst for milk— creatures as trusting toward their mother as they were unsuspecting— as if she were threatening strangers.
But when the Bodhisattva saw her, though he was steadfast, he trembled out of compassion due to the suffering of another, like the king of mountains at the shaking of the earth.
It is truly marvelous that those whose nature is compassion, having manifested fortitude even amidst their own great sufferings,
tremble at the slightest suffering of another.
Then the Bodhisattva, with words composed by the power of compassion that revealed his extraordinary nature and were uttered with hurried repetitions of syllables, said to his disciple:
"Child, child!
Behold the worthlessness of cyclic existence; even one's own children are sought as prey."
Having transgressed the boundaries of affection, she desires to eat out of hunger.
"Alas! How exceedingly cruel is this ferocity of self-love, by which even a mother desires to devour her own children!"
Who would wish to nourish the enemy consisting of self-attachment,
by which one might set foot even upon such deeds as these?
"Therefore, let some means to remedy her suffering from hunger be sought immediately, before she destroys her children and herself.
I too shall strive to restrain her from this act of desperation.
Having promised him "So be it," he set about searching for food for her.
Then the Bodhisattva, having dismissed that disciple with an excuse, fell into reflection:
"While my entire body is present, why do I seek flesh from another?
For the attainment of such a gain would be accidental for him, and likewise, this would be a failure of purpose for me."

Moreover: He who feels no joy when his body— which is soulless, subject to division, devoid of essence, suffering, ungrateful, and perpetually impure— is being employed for the sake of another, is not a wise man.
Out of attachment to one's own happiness, the suffering of another is neglected either because of a lack of power or due to indifference;
yet, since I have no happiness while another suffers, and since I possess the power [to help], how could I remain indifferent?
If, despite having the power to do so, I were to remain indifferent even toward an assailant immersed in suffering,
my mind would burn as if I had committed a sin, like a great forest fire consuming dry undergrowth.
Therefore, by means of this body whose life has been surrendered to a fall from the riverbank,
I shall effect the protection of the doe from the slaughter of her son, and likewise protect her offspring from the presence of that [lion].
Furthermore:

"The sight of those who strive for the welfare of the world is an encouragement to those of feeble resolve, a source of joy for those skilled in renunciation, and an attraction for the minds of the virtuous. (AJm 1.26)
It causes despondency in the great army of Māra; it inspires confidence in those who love the qualities of a Buddha;
it gives rise to shame in those intent on their own self-interest, and in those whose souls are afflicted by envy and greed.
It inspires faith in those who rely on the supreme vehicle; it causes amazement in those who pride themselves on their renunciation;
it purifies the great path to heaven for those who delight in giving and rejoice in the merit of others.
"May I indeed bring about the welfare of others even with my own limbs"—this was the aspiration I held; may that now bear fruit, for supreme enlightenment is not far off.
Neither out of rivalry, nor from a desire for fame, nor from greed for heaven, nor for the sake of a kingdom,
nor even for my own ultimate happiness do I have such devotion as this, except for the accomplishment of the welfare of others.

Likewise, may I always possess the power to remove the suffering of the world and to bring about its happiness at the same time as he does, just as the sun possesses the power to dispel darkness and produce light.
Whether seen, heard, come to mind through recollection, touched, or even encountered in conversation—
may I constantly perform, in every possible way, deeds for the welfare of the world that are joined with happiness.
Having thus resolved to accomplish the welfare of others, he cast off his own body, experiencing joy even at the loss of life, and thereby astonishing the minds of even the steadfast deities.

Then that tigress, her curiosity and indignation aroused by the sound of the Bodhisattva’s body falling, desisted from her attempt to slaughter her own offspring and cast her eyes about. As soon as she saw the Bodhisattva’s body with its life-force departed, she rushed forward at once and began to devour it.
Then his disciple, having failed to find any meat, returned and, looking about for his teacher, saw the Bodhisattva’s body with its life-force departed being devoured by that young tigress.
He saw him;
and, his surge of grief and suffering dispelled by wonder at that excellence of action, as if pouring forth great respect for the refuge of those virtues, he spoke this to himself:
"Oh, how compassionate this man is toward people afflicted by calamity! Oh, how free from attachment to his own happiness is this Great-Souled One!"
Oh, how the state of the virtuous has been brought to its highest excellence! Oh, how the glory of fame of others has been crushed!
Oh, what supreme love has been displayed—heroic, free from fear, and the very refuge of virtue!
Oh, how this body, though composed of its own [ordinary] qualities, has been forcibly brought to the state of being a preeminent object of veneration!
"Alas! The indignation of this upholder of the earth, who is by nature so gentle, at the calamities of others;
alas! My own wickedness has been brought to light by this excellence of valor. (AJm 1.36)
Now that the world has come under the protection of this Lord, it truly need no longer grieve;
for today, the God of Love, agitated by the fear of defeat, will surely be intent on sighing deeply.
In every way, let there be homage to this illustrious one, the refuge of all beings, possessed of exceedingly vast compassion, the immeasurable being, the Bodhisattva in the true sense of the term.
Then he reported that matter to his fellow religious practitioners.

Thereupon, with their faces struck with wonder at that deed, his disciples, along with Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Bhujagas, and the lords of the gods, covered the earth where his bones lay with showers of garlands, garments, ornaments, and sandalwood powder. Thus the ground became strewn with them.

Thus, since even in previous births that Blessed One was one whose nature was characterized by supreme, unconditional affection for all sentient beings and who had become the very self of all living creatures, one should cultivate the highest faith in the Buddha, the Blessed One;
and by those in whom such faith has arisen, joy toward the Buddha, the Blessed One, should be generated.
"In this way, our faith is directed toward its proper object"—thus too should it be understood.
In that same way, the Dharma should be heard with reverence;

for it has been brought about through hundreds of difficult deeds, so it must likewise be spoken of in the praise of compassion—that compassion which accomplishes an excellence of intrinsic nature and is the cause for engaging in the act of benefiting others.
The First Tale: The Birth Story of the Tigress, from the Garland of Bodhisattva Avadānas.
2. The Śibi-jātaka: "This True Dharma was acquired by that Blessed One for our sake through hundreds of difficult deeds; therefore, it should be heard with reverence."
Thus it is heard: This Blessed One, while formerly a bodhisattva, having accumulated merit through deeds made habitual by practice over immeasurable time, once became the king of the Śibis.
From his very childhood, he delighted in attending upon the elderly, was devoted to discipline, and was beloved by his subjects; for he was naturally intelligent.

Possessing an intellect rendered exceedingly pure by the acquisition of manifold sciences, and endowed with enthusiasm, the power of mantras, personal prowess, and divine fortune, he protected his subjects as if they were his own children.
In him, the floods of virtues conducive to the three aims of life were established as if through the force of mutual joy.
They shone with all their forms intact, and their beauty was not marred by the agitation of conflict.
Like a mockery for the ill-behaved and arrogant, like a most grievous calamity for the small-minded,
that prosperity there became truly worthy of its name, being like wine to those of little soul.
On account of his noble nature, his quality of compassion, and his sovereignty over wealth,
that best of kings rejoiced in seeing the faces of supplicants, which possessed an untroubled radiance through the joy of having their desires fulfilled.

Then that king, out of his love for giving, caused alms-halls to be built all around the city, fully supplied with every requisite, wealth, and grain; and like a cloud at the beginning of the Kṛta age, he rained down a shower of gifts— befitting his own majesty, provided according to every desire, elegant with its refinements, charming, and auspicious because it was never untimely.
Food to those seeking food, drink to those seeking drink, and bedding, seating, clothing, meals, perfumes, garlands, gold, silver, and so forth to those seeking each of these.
Then, having heard of that king’s generosity and nobility, men dwelling in regions distinguished by various directions approached that land with hearts struck with wonder and filled with joy.
Having mentally traversed the entire world of men and finding no opportunity for their requests elsewhere,
those seekers approached him with faces brightened by delight, just as wild elephants approach a great lake.

Then that king, his eyes dilated with joy at the sight of the beggars— who approached from all sides with minds delighted by the hope of gain, their natural splendor concealed by the garb of travelers, like friends who had been long away—
welcomed their request as if it were pleasant news; and by giving, he conquered the seekers through the satisfaction they felt.
That fragrance arising from his generosity, consisting of renown, was scattered by the wind of the words of those who sought his aid;
it removed the pride of other kings, just as the scent of a fragrant elephant dispels the arrogance of rival elephants.

Then once, as that king was inspecting his halls of charity, he observed that because the seekers were already satisfied, the arrival of supplicants had become sparse; seeing this, he found no satisfaction, for he did not cease from the practice of giving.
That hero of generosity did not satisfy his thirst by the mere arrival of the seekers, but rather by actually granting their requests.
For no seeker was able to overcome his resolve to give by means of the magnitude of his request.
The thought occurred to him:
"How exceedingly fortunate are those distinguished noble beings to whom even their own limbs are requested by supplicants with such confidence and lack of restraint!
As for me, however, my suppliants have become so timid in their requests that they do not venture even to ask for mere wealth, as if they were terrified by the harsh words of rejection."
Then, perceiving that the king’s thought was fixed upon giving— having turned away from attachment even to his own limbs— the Earth trembled like a wife devoted to her husband.

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, wondering "What is this? as Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains—resplendent with the radiance of various jewels—trembled due to the shaking of the earth's surface, perceived that this extraordinary reflection of the king was caused by the earthquake; his heart overcome with wonder, he fell into deep thought.
With a mind uplifted by the intense joy of giving, what indeed was contemplated by the king,
who had girded himself with the belt of resolve for generosity and remained firm in his determination to give away his own body?
"I shall first investigate this matter."

Then, while that king was seated in his assembly hall surrounded by his circle of ministers, and after the customary proceedings had been completed, as the proclamation was being made to summon those who had petitions— asking "Who desires what?"— while the heaps of jewels, gold, silver, and wealth presided over by the treasurer were being opened,
and while the chests of garments, their interiors filled with various clothes, were having their covers loosened, they were brought forward.

When various kinds of vehicles were being driven by those skilled in managing them, and when a great multitude of supplicants had gathered around diverse and magnificent conveyances, Śakra, the lord of the gods, manifested in the form of an aged, blind brahmin and appeared within the king’s line of vision. Then the king, as if rising to meet him and embracing him with a mind permeated by compassion and loving-kindness— steadfast, serene, and gentle— welcomed him.
As if invited by the king’s attendants with the words, “What is your purpose? he approached the presence of the monarch and, preceded by words of victory and blessing, spoke thus to the king:
“O foremost of kings, an old man has come from afar, seeking the sight of your eyes.”
For even with a single glance, O lotus-eyed Lord of the World, the course of worldly affairs may be understood.

Then the Bodhisattva, experiencing a supreme festival of joy through the fulfillment of his most cherished desire, reflected: "Is this which was spoken by the brahmin actually true, or have I merely conceived it so through the habit of mental construction?
With a mind thus stirred by reflection and parched with the longing to hear the pleasant words of the request for his eyes, he spoke to that beggar for his eyes.
"By whom were you instructed, O foremost of brahmins, that you have come here to beg my eyes?
Whose reputation for saying 'the eye is very difficult to give' has reached me?"
Then Śakra, wearing the guise of a brahmin, having understood the king's intention, said:
"I have come here to beg for your eye at the instruction of Śakra, who is like Śakra himself.
Make his high regard and my own hope fruitful by the gift of your eye."

Then that king, thinking from Śakra’s proclamation, "Surely this brahmin shall obtain the perfection of sight through the power of the deity by means of this ritual," spoke to him with words clear with joy:
"O brahmin, I shall fulfill for you that very desire for which you have approached me.
To you who so desires it, I give one eye; indeed, I shall give you even both eyes."

Go now, O you whose face is adorned with eyes like blossomed blue lotuses, before the people gaze upon you and are tossed on the swing of doubt, wondering, "Is this he or is it not? and then, as their wonder arises, exclaiming, "This is indeed he! (AJm 2.14).

Then the king’s ministers, having learned of his resolve to give away his eyes, their minds distressed by agitation, alarm, and despair, said to the king: "Out of excessive joy for giving, you have failed to consider this misconduct that will result in harm;
be gracious, O Lord, do not do this—indeed, you ought not to give away your eyes."
Do not cast us all away for the sake of this one brahmin;
enough with burning our subjects—who have been raised in comfort—with the fire of grief.
Bestow riches that awaken prosperity, glorious jewels, and milch-cows; grant chariots yoked with well-trained horses, and elephants graced by the playful splendor of intoxication.

"Grant houses that resound with the tinkling of anklets, possessing a splendor exceeding autumnal clouds and providing comfort in all seasons; do not give away your own eye, O sole eye of the world! AJm_2.18 //
Furthermore, let this be considered, O Great King:
how indeed can the eye belonging to one person be applied to another?
Or if this is the power of destiny, why does it have regard for your own eye?
Moreover, O King:
"What use has a poor man for eyes that merely witness the prosperity of others?
Therefore, O King, give him wealth; do not commit such a rash act."
Then the king spoke to those ministers with words that were both conciliatory and sweet:
"He who, having declared 'I shall give,' then sets his mind on not giving, fastens upon himself the loosened noose of greed. (AJm 2.21)
Having made the promise "I shall give," he who then turns his mind otherwise due to stinginess and an irresolute intellect—who could be more sinful than him? (AJm 2.22)
There is no atonement for speech that is harsh due to breaking one's word, having made a promise to give after first steadying the hopes of those who seek.
Furthermore, regarding what was said—that why does he not possess sight solely through the power of the deity—listen to this:
"Indeed, it is observed that effects are not accomplished by a single cause alone;
for even a divine ordinance must depend upon other causes. (AJm 2.24)
Therefore, you ought not to exert yourselves to obstruct this preeminent gift of mine.
The ministers said:

"We have informed [Your Majesty] that it is fitting for Your Majesty to give wealth, grain, jewels, and the like, but not one's own eye; therefore, we do not wish to lead Your Majesty astray at an improper occasion. The king said:

"Whatever is requested, that alone one should give; what is undesired does not please when given here in this world. What use is water to one who is already being carried by it? Therefore, I shall give him the object he has prayed for."
Then, a chief minister of that king—one whose intimacy and affection were deeply rooted, who out of the force of his devotion disregarded all formal etiquette—spoke thus to the king:
"O Sire, do not do this!

That which cannot be attained by anyone through the practice of even slight austerity or meditative concentration, and having reached which one may obtain both fame and heaven through hundreds of numerous sacrifices—"
Having attained this kingship that rivals the majesty of Śakra, what have you seen that you wish to give away your eyes? What manner of person is this, and from where does such a custom originate?
Having obtained an opportunity among the gods through sacrifices, shining on all sides with renown,
and having your feet colored by the luster of the crest-jewels of kings— what is it that you desire that you give away your eye?
Then the king spoke with conciliation to that minister:
"This effort is not for the sake of attaining universal sovereignty, nor for heaven, nor for liberation, nor for fame;
rather, this devotion of mine is for the sake of protecting the worlds, so that the hardship of his begging may not be in vain."

Then that king, having slowly extracted one eye—which possessed the lovely luster of a blue lotus petal—without injury, according to the procedure prescribed by the physician, gave it with supreme joy to the petitioner for eyes.
Thereupon, Śakra, the lord of the gods, performed such a feat of supernatural power (*ṛddhyabhisaṃskāra*) that the king, together with his retinue, saw that very eye re-established in its place.
Then, beholding the eye-seeker with one eye opened, the king, his heart overflowing with supreme joy, bestowed the second eye upon him as well.

Then that king, his face resembling a lotus-pool where his eyes were the lotuses, attained a joy unparalleled by the citizens; and the twice-born man beheld him with his sight restored in its entirety.
Then, in the inner apartments and throughout the city of the lord of men, the earth was drenched on all sides with tears of grief;
but Śakra was filled with wonder and attained supreme satisfaction upon beholding the king’s unshakable resolve for perfect enlightenment.
Then, Śakra’s heart overcome with wonder, this thought occurred to him:
"Oh, what steadfastness! Oh, what courage! Oh, what desire for the welfare of beings!
Even though this deed is before my very eyes, it seems to provoke reflection."
Therefore, this marvelous being ought not to endure such suffering for long; for I shall strive to restore his sight by demonstrating the proper means.
Then, as that king’s eye-wound gradually healed and the grief of the women of his harem and the people of the city and countryside had subsided and thinned,

he desired solitude; while he was seated cross-legged on the bank of a garden pond— where the trees were bent low with the weight of their blossoms, where a soft, fragrant, cool, and pleasant breeze blew, and which resounded with the humming of swarms of bees— the divine Śakra, Lord of the Devas, appeared before him.
When questioned by the king, "Who is this?", he replied:
"I am Śakra, the lord of the gods, who has come into your presence. Welcome! Please command me; what is your purpose?"
Addressed with such courtesy, he spoke again to the king:
"Choose a boon, O royal sage; let whatever you desire be spoken."
Then that king, because he was accustomed to giving and unpracticed in the path of the wretchedness of begging, spoke with fortitude, composure, and heroism:
"O Śakra, my wealth is abundant and my great power is effective;
yet, because of my blindness, death alone now appeals to me."
O Indra, because I do not see the faces of supplicants— whose desires have been fully satisfied and whose eyes are overflowing with joy and faith— I prefer death.
Śakra said:
"Enough of this resolve of yours;
only such as you, O noble being, attain things of this kind."
Moreover, I ask you this:
now that you have been reduced to such a state by supplicants, how indeed is your mind toward them? Tell me that, for it is not right to conceal it, so that you may attain a state worthy of trust.
The king said: "What is this persistence of yours, sir, in trying to provoke us?
Moreover, O Lord of the Gods, listen:
both then and now, the words of supplicants consist of the same fixed syllables of entreaty."
Just as my beloveds are like personified blessings, so may my one eye open.

Then, by the power of that king’s solemn vow (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*) and the particular excellence of his accumulated merit, immediately upon these words, one eye appeared— resembling the petal of a blue lotus, with its center as if covered by a fragment of sapphire. When that wondrous eye had appeared, the king, his mind filled with joy, spoke again to Śakra:
And as for that one who begged me for a single eye, having joyfully bestowed both eyes upon him with a mind solely intent on the festival of affection— may my second eye likewise become such as his.
Then, immediately upon his speaking, a second eye appeared for that king as if in rivalry with that [first] eye.
Thereupon, the earth, together with its mountains, trembled; the ocean surged, overstepping its shores;
and the drums of the gods resounded with deep and enchanting tones.
His body, lovely with serenity, was seen to shine with purity like the sun in autumn;
and a wondrous rain of flowers, colored by swirling sandalwood powder, fell from the vault of the sky.
The gods, accompanied by throngs of Apsarases, arrived there with eyes blossoming in wonder;
a breeze of pleasing quality blew, and joy expanded within the minds of all living beings.
Proclaimed by hosts of beings of great supernatural power, their minds filled with joy and wonder,
auspicious words were heard on all sides praising the king’s extraordinary deeds.

"Oh, what magnanimity! Oh, what compassion! Behold the purity of this mind! Oh, how the intellect is indifferent toward its own pleasures! Homage be to you, whose fortitude and prowess are so utterly marvelous! (AJm_2.42)
The world has truly attained a protector through you, who possess the splendor of a fully blossomed lotus-eye;
indeed, the accumulations of merit have at last become fruitful, for by means of Dharma, victory has been mightily won after a long time.
Then Śakra, having cheered him with the words "Excellent! Excellent!", spoke to him again:
"O King, your pure-hearted intention was not unknown to us.
Nevertheless, O monarch, these two eyes have been restored to you by me."
And for these two of yours, there will be an unimpeded power to see everything within a hundred yojanas all around, even if it is obscured by mountains.
Having said this, Śakra vanished right there.

Then the Bodhisattva, followed by ministers whose minds were filled with wonder and joy and whose eyes were wide open and blinking slowly, and being gazed upon by the citizens, was greeted by Brahmins who preceded him with words of victory and blessing;
he proceeded toward the excellent city, which was adorned with raised banners and variegated flags and displayed the splendor of a great festival.

Having approached and sat down in the assembly, for the sake of pleasing the brahmins, elders, and citizens led by the chief minister who had come there, he taught them this Dharma concerning his own life:
"Who indeed in this world would be lax in their devotion toward performing with wealth what is dear to those who come as supplicants?"
Having beheld these two eyes of mine, endowed with divine power, obtained through the merit of my past gifts.
Even though it is hidden by many mountains beyond a hundred yojanas,
I see clearly from every direction that which is situated not far away.

What means for higher rebirth is superior to the gift born of discipline and compassion for others, by which, having given away my human eye right here, I have obtained a superhuman, divine eye? (AJm 2.48)
Having understood this, O Śibis, make wealth fruitful through gifts and enjoyment;
for this is the path in both this world and the next for one whose primary aim is renown and the arising of happiness.
Of wealth, which is essentially void and trivial, its true essence is that which is given away by one intent on the welfare of the world;
for that which is being given becomes a treasure, whereas that which is not given results solely in destruction.
Therefore, since this True Dharma was acquired for our sake by that Blessed One through hundreds of such difficult feats, it should be listened to with reverence.

Furthermore, the greatness of the Tathāgata should be recounted here as before, as well as the praise of his compassion; and likewise, in demonstrating the fruit of merit, it should be shown how merits accumulated with such reverence manifest even in this very life a mere flower of one’s own power—a charming succession of fame.
The second [tale], the Śibi-jātaka.
3. The *Kulmāṣapiṇḍī-jātaka*:
There is no gift, however small, that does not yield great fruit, whether it arises from a pure heart or is offered with an excellent vessel.
Thus it is heard: when the Blessed One was a bodhisattva, he became the sovereign of Kośala.
While his royal qualities—such as the excellence of his energy, counsel, majesty, and power—were already preeminent, the splendor of his divine endowments surpassed even their manifestation.
His virtues, adorned by the excellence of his divine nature, shone forth even more brilliantly,
like the rays of the moon when its beauty has blossomed in autumn.

He abandoned even his arrogant enemies, while Fortune, as if with redened cheeks, took delight in those who sought refuge with him; thus his sovereignty followed the dictates of both his wrath and his favor toward other kings.
Because his very nature was righteousness, his mind never harbored any ill-will toward others that would cause them harm;
yet his devotion to his servants flourished in such a way that Fortune no longer took pleasure in his enemies.
He recollected his own birth that had just passed away;

and through that recollection, being moved by a sense of spiritual urgency, he bestowed gifts upon ascetics, brahmins, the destitute, and beggars as a primary cause for the attainment of happiness, giving more excellently than before.
Furthermore, he undertook the restraint of moral discipline and the observance of the *poṣadha* on the days of the lunar festivals.

Desiring to establish the world in the highest good by manifesting the power of his own merit in the royal assembly and within his own harem, he, with a confident heart, spoke these two verses of certain meaning:
"Not even the slightest service rendered to the Sugata can result in such a meager display of fruit as was previously heard;
behold now this greatness of the abundance of fruit from a mere lump of sour gruel—saltless, parched, coarse, and reddish. (AJm 3.4)

Behold the excellence of the harvest of my grain-porridge: this army of mine, diverse with chariots and horses and possessing the grace of rutting lordly elephants; this entire earth; abundant wealth; devoted prosperity; noble wives; and all these things. (3.5)

Although the ministers, the elder brahmins, and the leading citizens were filled with curiosity, they did not dare to question him as to what the Great King had in mind when he repeatedly spoke these two verses.

Then, because of her affection for the king, the queen—whose confidence, intimacy, and favor were entirely unimpeded—her curiosity aroused by the course of the conversation, questioned him in the assembly:
"O Lord of Men, you speak as if pouring forth the joy residing in your heart;
my own heart is filled with curiosity regarding that which you have told me."
Therefore, this person ought to hear it, O King, if you would explain what it is that you speak;
for such a secret is not proclaimed anywhere, and because of this, I too am asking about it openly.
Then the king, gazing at the queen with an exceedingly affectionate look of love, spoke with a face blossoming with a smile.
Having heard this outburst of mine regarding the meaning of the unmanifest sign,
it is not only your mind that is stirred by curiosity in this matter.
This entire circle of ministers has their minds reeling with curiosity, as does the city together with its inner apartments; therefore, hear from me the reason why I speak thus.

Like one awakened from a dream, I remember my birth; in this very city, I was once a laborer, and though endowed with virtuous conduct, my wretched livelihood was earned through the performance of work for those exalted only by their wealth.
Thus, desiring to enter into service— a hall of humiliation, toil, and wretchedness— out of hope for protection and out of fear of lacking a livelihood,
I saw four ascetics seeking alms, their senses subdued and appearing as if followed by the very splendor of mendicancy.
Having bowed to them with a mind softened by faith, I, being self-restrained, gave them a mere portion of boiled grain in my own home;
this present state of mine is like the sprouting of its seed, in that the radiance from the crests of other kings is now cast upon the dust of my feet.
It is with this very intention in mind, O Queen, that I say:
"I can never have enough of merits, nor of the sight of the Arhats. (AJm 3.13)
Then the queen, her eyes wide with joy and wonder, looking up at the king with great respect, said:
"This particular excellence of the arising of the ripening of merit is truly worthy of such merit;
and it is fitting for the Great King, who has witnessed the fruit of merit himself, that you have such devotion toward meritorious deeds."
Thus, turning away from the practice of evil, like a father toward his subjects, well-disposed toward their proper protection and intent upon the acquisition of meritorious virtues;

blazing with the glory of fame and the abundance of your generosity, with your commands firmly established upon the heads of rival kings, protect for a long time the earth— clothed in the ocean-waters folded by the wind— according to the way of Dharma.
The king said: "How could this not be so, O Queen?
Therefore, I shall strive once more to take refuge in that very path to the highest good, whose beautiful signs have been clearly perceived.
For when people, having heard of the fruit of giving, offer it to others, why should I not, having observed my own state, give what is within me?"
Then the king, gazing most affectionately upon the queen—who blazed with splendor like a goddess—his heart filled with curiosity regarding the cause of her magnificent fortune, spoke again:
"O auspicious lady, you shine in the midst of women like the crescent moon among the stars; what deed, indeed, have you performed that results in such exceedingly sweet prosperity?"
The goddess said: "O Lord, there is something that I too remember from my previous birth.
When she was thus respectfully questioned by the king, saying, "Tell me, tell me now," she spoke:
"I remember it as if experienced in childhood, when I was a maidservant, [seeing] a single portion of cooked rice that had been set aside."
Having respectfully offered [this] to the Sage whose outflows were exhausted, I fell asleep there and have now awakened here.
"I remember this merit, O god among men, by which I have attained lordship over the earth together with you;
for as the Sage said, 'Among those whose outflows are exhausted, not even the slightest thing is done'—just so you have spoken. (AJm 3.18)

Then the king, perceiving that the assembly—having conceived great respect for meritorious deeds through the demonstration of their fruits—was now serene in mind and singularly filled with wonder, reflected: "Seeing such an extensive splendor of ripened fortune resulting from even a small amount of virtue, who indeed would not be intent on performing meritorious acts through the practice of generosity and moral conduct?
That man, even if he possesses sufficient wealth, is not capable of seeing this, his mind shrouded by the darkness of stinginess, who does not attain glory through gifts. (AJm 3.19)

If one who is helpless must give up wealth that serves no purpose for anyone, and if by giving that wealth according to what is right he might manifest some virtue—what person, knowing the essence of virtues, would resort to a path of envy? For the various qualities such as joy and the like, which follow from fame, are the established virtues of generosity.
Generosity is indeed a great treasure that follows one, not shared with thieves and the like; it is the washing away of the dust of the faults of stinginess and greed from the mind.
Generosity removes the fatigue of the path of saṃsāra; generosity is a comfortable vehicle, a most excellent friend who is well-disposed and provides many comforts. (AJm 3.21)

Whether it be the accumulation of wealth, radiant sovereignty, residence in the city of the Thirty-three gods, or the excellence of physical beauty—whatever one desires, all that is obtained through giving. Considering this well-ascertained truth, who would not give gifts? AJm_3.22 //
They say that giving is the extraction of the essence from riches; they say that giving is the foundation of sovereign powers.
Giving is the glorious deed of a virtuous person; it is not a gift of dust that is a true gift for those of little wisdom.
Then that assembly, having with great reverence rejoiced at those persuasive words of the king, became intent upon the practice of virtues such as generosity.
Thus, there is no gift that is insignificant when it arises from clarity of mind and is bestowed upon an excellent recipient, because of the greatness of its maturation.
Therefore, one who gives with a clear mind to the Noble Saṅgha—the unsurpassed field of merit—should generate supreme joy, thinking:
"Such success as this is not far off for me, and even more distinguished than this."
The third is the Kulmāṣapiṇḍī Jātaka.
4. In the *Śreṣṭhijātaka*, it is said that virtuous persons desire to give even without considering their own loss;
by what person who is healthy would it not be right to give?
Thus it is heard: When the Blessed One was a bodhisattva, he had attained vast wealth and prosperity through his extraordinary merit and excellence of exertion;

because of his character of practicing fair dealings, he became an object of great esteem for the world; he was born into a noble lineage, and his intellect was exceedingly pure through his mastery of various branches of knowledge and the arts.

Through the greatness of his virtues, the merchant received the highest honors from the king; and because of his habitual generosity, his wealth became common to all people. His name, exalted by his heroic liberality, was proclaimed here and there by supplicants with joyful hearts, and it pervaded the ten directions.
In that matter, the petitioner’s mind was not wavering on the swing of doubt as to whether he should give or not;
for toward him, whose noble deeds were renowned, the multitude of supplicants maintained a bold intimacy born of confidence.
He did not protect his wealth for the sake of his own pleasure, nor out of rivalry, nor from being overcome by greed;
rather, he was unable to endure the suffering of those who sought it, and thus he protected it only so as not to have to say, "It is not here."

Then once, at the time of that Great Being's meal, when he had bathed and anointed himself, a Pratyekabuddha—whose fuel of all afflictions had been consumed by the fire of wisdom and who desired to increase his store of merit—came to his house seeking alms. It was a time when a variety of foods, including hard and soft dishes, had been prepared by a skillful cook; they were excellent, endowed with the qualities of color, fragrance, taste, and texture.
Having approached, he stood at the gateway,
looking a yoke’s length ahead upon the earth with a gaze that was fearless,
steady, and serene; there he remained, born of tranquility, his lotus-like fingertips resting upon his alms-bowl.

Then Māra, the Evil One, unable to endure that perfection of the Bodhisattva’s generosity, created for the purpose of obstructing it a hell between the Venerable One and the threshold of the door— a pit many fathoms deep, with a belly like blazing coals, terrifying to behold, with a fearsome roar, and filled with hundreds of writhing beings.
Then the Bodhisattva, seeing that a Pratyekabuddha had arrived seeking alms, said to his wife, "My lady,
give the noble one almsfood yourself.
Having agreed to this, saying "So be it," she took excellent food and drink and set out.
Beholding hell, she suddenly turned back from the vicinity of the gate, her eyes trembling with fear and despair.
When questioned by her husband, "What is this?", she, though her throat was choked by sudden terror, somehow managed to explain it to him.

Then the Bodhisattva, thinking with agitation, "How can this noble one depart from my house without having received alms? disregarded what she had said and, taking exquisite food and drink himself, approached the vicinity of the gateway with the desire to offer alms to that Great Being; there he beheld that most terrifying intermediate hell.
As he was wondering, "What indeed is this?", Māra the Evil One emerged from the wall of his palace, displayed a divine and wondrous form, and standing in the air,
spoke as if desiring his welfare: "Householder, this is the great hell named Mahāraurava."
Those who, enticed by the donor's words of praise, destroy wealth through the vice of giving,
shall dwell for many thousands of autumns in this place from which departure is difficult to obtain.
Wealth is the specific cause for the three aims of life; when that is destroyed, by whom is Dharma not destroyed?
And having destroyed Dharma by the eradication of wealth, how indeed could one not be established in hell?
Because you have committed this sin by destroying the root of the Dharma in your pursuit of gain through the practice of giving,
this mouth of the Destroyer of Hell has risen up from here to devour you, with its fierce tongue of flame.
Therefore, it is well that you restrain your mind from giving; for in this way, there would be no immediate downfall for you.
Do not become equal to these givers who are struggling and weeping piteously.
But the recipient, having ceased the removal of what was given, attains the state of a god.
Therefore, desisting from obstructing the path to heaven, take recourse in self-restraint through the exertion of giving.

Then the Bodhisattva, realizing that this was surely an effort by that evil-minded one to obstruct his giving, spoke to him with certainty, his voice uninterrupted by sweet syllables of firm discipline and self-possession:
"This noble path has been shown to us by you, who are skillful in looking after our welfare."
And especially toward the deities, their conduct was characterized by supreme compassion for others.
It is proper to proceed along the path of pacification either before the arising of a fault or immediately after it;
for once a disease has progressed due to the faults of improper conduct, the application of medical treatment is merely a futile effort.
And I suspect this addiction to giving of mine has passed beyond the scope of medical treatment;
for even disregarding your well-wishing, my mind does not shrink from bestowing gifts.

As for what you have said—that there is unrighteousness in giving, and that wealth is the specific cause of righteousness—this human intellect of mine does not understand it; for apart from giving, the path of righteousness is not true to its purpose.
Whether being deposited as a cause for merit, or being forcibly plundered by thieves,
or with its form submerged within the belly of a flood, it has become food for the fire.
"Since the giver of wealth goes to hell while the recipient goes to the world of the lord of gods,
this effort of mine toward giving has been further increased by you, even though you were restraining me."
"May these words of yours be unfailing, and may my supplicants go to heaven;
for this gift of mine is desired for the sake of the world's welfare, not as a means to achieve my own happiness."
Then Māra spoke again to the Bodhisattva with a steady hand, as if seeking his welfare: "Consider these words of mine as either beneficial advice or mere fickleness; go wherever you wish.
Whether endowed with happiness or filled with regret, you shall remember me with great respect."
The Bodhisattva said:
"O noble one, may you forgive me!
I would willingly fall into hell, with its flickering and fierce fires, with my head bowed low and consumed by the mass of flames."
But I shall not take away [the wealth] from those supplicants who have shown their friendship through their entreaties, by treating them with contempt at the very time they seek my honor.

Having spoken thus, the Bodhisattva—sustained by the power of his own good fortune and knowing the absence of any fault in giving—shook off his kinsmen and attendants who were intent solely on dissuading him; with a mind unassailed by fear and his desire to give further increased, he proceeded through the midst of the hells.
Then, by the power of his merit, a lotus free from mud appeared for him there.
He laughed at Māra as if in contempt, with his row of filament-teeth that were white like the filaments of a lotus.
Then the Bodhisattva, having approached the Pratyekabuddha by means of a lotus-bridge produced from the excellence of his own merit, offered him alms-food with a heart filled with serene joy.
Then, in order to awaken his serene confidence, the monk leapt up into the sky;
raining and blazing, he shone there with the splendor of a cloud illuminated by lightning.
But Māra, his desires crushed and his splendor stolen, was overcome by despondency;
unable to bear looking at him face to face, he vanished along with his hell.
What is this that has been brought forward? Even disregarding such a transgression, virtuous men desire to give;
indeed, who that is healthy would not give?
Those who possess courage cannot be made to go the wrong way even out of fear; thus it should also be applied.
The Fourth Birth Story: The Merchant.
5. The Jātaka of the Merchant Aviṣahya:
Virtuous persons do not fall into a deficiency of giving out of fear for the loss of their wealth, nor out of a desire for prosperity.

Thus it is heard: There was once a merchant who was the most excellent of givers; he was endowed with a multitude of virtues such as renunciation, ethical discipline, noble lineage, self-restraint, learning, wisdom, and freedom from pride; he was like Kubera in his wealth and prosperity; because he welcomed all guests, he never ceased his practice of giving; and he was devoted to the welfare of the world.
Invincible because he was immune to the defects of stinginess and the like, he was known by the name Avishahya (the Invincible).
Because he destroyed any hesitation regarding the attainment of desired goals, he was a specific cause for the awakening of joy;
just as the sight of him brought delight to those seeking wealth, so too did the sight of him bring delight to those seeking the Dharma.
When addressed with the fixed request "Give," he was unable to say "I have nothing," for his attachment to wealth had been deprived of its place in his heart by great compassion.
As the essence of his wealth was being carried away by supplicants from his house, he experienced even greater joy;
for he understood that those riches were fierce and dense misfortunes, destined for swift destruction without cause.
The worldly interests of people are for the most part based on greed and lead to the path of miserable rebirths;
yet his own interests, because they brought about the prosperity of both himself and others, shone forth as truly worthy of their name.

Then, as that Great Being was completely satisfying the crowd of supplicants from all sides with vast distributions of wealth— given according to their desires, without affliction, and adorned by the refined conduct of the virtuous— the Lord Śakra, King of the Devas, his mind overcome with wonder upon hearing of such noble generosity, sought to test the firmness of his resolve regarding giving; thus, every day, he [concealed] the entire collection of his wealth, grain, jewels, and household goods.
He caused each of those things to disappear, thinking, "Perhaps he might be led into stinginess by the fear that his wealth would be exhausted.
However, as for the Great Being who was resolutely intent on giving...
Just as his wealth perished like droplets of water cast by the sun,
even so he drew it forth from his house, which was as if ablaze, by means of vast gifts.

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, perceiving that the Great Being was solely intent on renunciation, became even more astonished; and although his wealth and essence were being depleted, he caused all of it to vanish in a single night, with the exception of a coil of rope and a single sickle.
Then, when the night had turned to dawn, the Bodhisattva woke as was his custom and beheld his own residence empty of wealth, grain, furnishings, and attendants;
it was silent and desolate, as if despoiled by *rākṣasas*, its appearance no longer pleasing. With the thought "What is this?
arising within him, he began to investigate and saw there only that coil of rope and the sickle.
A thought occurred to him:
"If someone who lives by his own prowess, using improper words to ask for something, has shown such affection toward my house, then my wealth has indeed been well-employed.
But if now, due to the fault of my own misfortune, they—unable to endure my rising prosperity—have fled elsewhere without even using it, then that is a tragedy."
The fickleness of wealth has been known by me even from before;
however, it is the very distress of those who seek it that now burns my heart.

Having long been accustomed to the pleasures of giving and hospitality, how indeed will those who seek my wealth fare now that they have approached my home destitute of riches, like thirsty ones come to a dried-up lake? (AJm 5.7)

Then the Bodhisattva, through the support of his own fortitude, remained untouched by the dejection of despondency; yet, because he had not practiced the manner of begging even in that state, he did not dare to ask others for alms, even those who were familiar to him.
Thinking thus how difficult it was to beg, his compassion for the people who were supplicants became even greater.

Then that Great Being, out of regard for performing such acts as welcoming supplicants, personally took up that coil of rope and the sickle, and every day, with whatever small measure of wealth obtained from the sale of grass, he honored those who came to him with gifts and hospitality.

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, observing his lack of despondency even in the face of extreme poverty and his inclination toward giving, stood in the air with a body displaying divine and wondrous splendor; filled with wonder and great respect, he addressed that Great Being, seeking to dissuade him from his generosity: "Householder!"
Having reached this state that causes distress to the minds of your friends,
you have had your wealth seized neither by bandits, nor by water or fire, nor by kings, despite your excessive giving.
Therefore, out of regard for your welfare, I say this to you: restrain your passion for the vice of giving.
Even if, having come to such a state, you should not give, you will once again attain the splendor of your former prosperity.
Having observed that collyrium is exhausted over time even with constant, sparing use,
while anthills grow through accumulation, those who desire increase find that self-restraint alone is the path.
Then the Bodhisattva, demonstrating the greatness of the practice of giving, said to Śakra:
"O Thousand-eyed One, it is exceedingly difficult for a noble person to act ignobly, even when in great distress.
O Śakra, let me not possess such wealth that, for the sake of acquiring it, I might become one whose heart is base."
Since there is a path that serves as an antidote to suffering, by which those who desire it may go through the death of their begging,
what man who considers himself a son of noble family would strike those afflicted ones with the dry thunderbolt of saying, "It does not exist"?

What indeed would one like me take from that—be it a jewel, wealth, or even sovereignty in heaven—if, by the distress of begging, he were to cause the faces of supplicants to lose their luster? AJm_5.13 //

One who would increase the accumulation of the fault of stinginess, or who would not cultivate a mind of renunciation—he deserves only to be abandoned by those like me; he is a calamity disguised as the appearance of possession.
Since wealth is as fickle as the dance of a flash of lightning, common to all, and a cause for manifold calamities—
while generosity is the very source of the arising of happiness— what noble person would resort to stinginess?

"O Śakra, you have shown me this self-sacrifice; I am moved by your compassionate concern for my welfare. But how could one whose mind is intensely accustomed to joy find restraint when it is directed toward such a noble path?"
And you ought not to apply your mind to the path of following after resentment in this matter;
for it is not possible to ascend the difficult terrain that opposes one's own nature with little strength.

Śakra said: "Householder, for one whose wealth is sufficient, whose treasuries and granaries are full, whose various and extensive enterprises are properly conducted, whose fortune has grown in the world, and who has brought sovereignty under his control— this course of events does not lead to such a state."
Behold him who has attained [this state]:

by means of auspicious karma, whether through the exercise of his own intellect, or through fame, or through conduct befitting his lineage, he has drawn forth prosperity and, like the sun, has overwhelmed the splendor of his rivals.

Having extended his courtesy through conversation with the people and awakened joy among his friends and kinsmen, he received honors even from the king; thus, as if embraced by the Goddess of Fortune herself out of her own desire, he was filled with longing.

Now, one whose efforts are fully exerted toward giving incurs neither the censure of people regarding pleasures, nor does he suffer the frustration of one with undeveloped wings wishing to ascend into the sky—provided it is not through the mere desire to give. (AJm 5.20)
Therefore, let wealth first be acquired through the support of self-restraint and composure; enough with the desire to give it away!
For what indeed could be more ignoble than that one should not give when riches have become non-existent?
The Bodhisattva said: "Enough of this excessive persistence on your part.
Even for one for whom their own interest is more important than the welfare of others, that person should give even by disregarding their own prosperity."
For he does not attain that joy through even great prosperity or through gifts; rather, he enjoys that satisfaction which comes from the conquest of greed.

Since one does not go to heaven by wealth alone, and since one attains holy renown through giving alone, and since one does not overcome faults such as envy [without it], who then would not devote themselves to giving for that reason? (AJm 5.23)
He who desires even his own self out of compassion in order to protect the worlds overwhelmed by old age and death—
he who finds no relish in his own pleasures because of the sufferings of others— what purpose would there be for him in wealth, even if it were as vast as yours?
Moreover, O Lord of Gods, just as the stability of wealth is transient, so too is the duration of life;
thus, having encountered a supplicant, one should not look toward one's own prosperity.
When one chariot makes a path upon the earth, another follows it even more boldly, and yet another as well;
my mind, however, having cast aside this first, auspicious way, finds no pleasure in following a path that leads to ruin.
And if my wealth should increase further, he will certainly rob me of the minds of beggars;
even when this happens, O Śakra, I shall give according to my means, and let us not be negligent in our commitment to generosity.
When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, his mind thoroughly pacified, greeted him with "Excellent! Excellent! and, looking upon him with great respect and affection, spoke:

"Even by means of deeds that are rivals to one's reputation—deeds that are base and cruel—people seek prosperity, being led astray by a fickle mind and, through attachment to their own pleasure, disregarding the consequences."
Without considering the loss of wealth, the sacrifice of your own happiness, or my own deception, you—
whose mind is resolute in accomplishing the welfare of others— have manifested the greatness of your own excellence.
Oh, how the heart of this one who shines with such extraordinary magnanimity has been cleared of the darkness of stinginess!
For even when his wealth was lost, it did not become deformed by the contraction of giving, nor did his intention waver.
And it is no wonder here that you, who suffer at the suffering of others, out of the power of compassion and desiring the welfare of the world,
were not shaken by me through the act of giving— just as a snow-white mountain peak is not shaken by the wind.
I have kept this wealth of yours hidden in order to test you and manifest your fame;
for a gem, even if it possesses great luster, would not otherwise attain the high value of a jewel’s renown.
Therefore, rain down upon supplicants with gifts, filling them as a great cloud fills the lakes;
you shall not suffer the loss of wealth through my protection, and you should forgive this conduct of mine.
Having thus gratified him, Śakra withdrew his essence of wealth from him, asked for his forgiveness, and vanished right there.
Thus, in this way, virtuous persons do not fall into a deficiency in giving, whether out of regard for the depletion of their wealth or out of a desire for prosperity.
The fifth is the Aviṣahya-Śreṣṭhi-jātaka.
6. The Śaśajātaka:
It is observed that even for Great Beings who have entered the animal realm, there is an engagement in giving according to their capacity;
by what person, then, being human, should it not be given?

Thus it is heard: In a certain forest region, dense with charming shrubs, grasses, and trees, abounding in flowers and fruits, its borders adorned by a river carrying pure, blue, lapis-lazuli-colored water,
its ground beautiful to behold and pleasant to the touch like a carpet of soft green turf, frequented by ascetics— there [he dwelt].
The Bodhisattva became a hare.
By virtue of his spiritual application, the perfection of his body, the excellence of his strength, and his vast vital energy,
he moved about that place with the grace of a king of beasts, unobserved by small animals and free from fear.
Clad in his own skin as an antelope hide and wearing the bark of his own body hair,
he shone there like a sage with a contented mind, surrounded by blades of grass and sprouts.
By his mental, vocal, and physical actions, purified by loving-kindness, his pupils— whose wickedness was subdued— became for the most part as gentle as deer.
Three companions—a water-dog (*udra*), a jackal, and a monkey—became bound to him with hearts especially affected by a profound affection and respect born of his preeminent virtues.
Like kinsmen whose love was tied together by mutual relationship, and like friends whose friendship had grown through mutual kindness and honor, they dwelt there in great joy.
Turning away from the nature of beasts, they practiced compassion toward living beings; through the pacification of greed, they forgot their inclination toward theft.

And by their conduct which followed the Dharma, by their sharpness of discernment, and by their movements which were disciplined, restrained, and steady, they became a source of wonder even to the gods.
[They were] in a manner that was conducive to happiness yet obstructed virtue, and in a manner that was favorable to virtue yet impeded happiness.
Even a human being shines by resorting to the side of virtue; how much more so, then, one who possesses the form of an animal!
But for them, there arose a virtuous teacher in the form of a hare, a master whose primary path was compassion for others;
and because his natural excellence followed the sequence of his qualities, his fame reached even the world of the gods.

Then once, at the time of evening, that Great-souled One was being reverently attended by those companions who had approached for the purpose of hearing the Dharma; together with them, he beheld the moon risen on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, its orb nearly full, its beauty enhanced by its distance from the sun, like a silver mirror without a handle, its disc slightly tilted to one side.
Having looked at his companions, he said:
"The moon, as if smiling with its perfectly full orb, announces to the virtuous the festival of the Poṣadha."

It is clear that tomorrow is the fifteenth day; therefore, while you are fulfilling the Poṣadha observance, you should sustain your lives by honoring guests who arrive at the proper time with special food obtained through righteous means.
Behold!
Since unions end in separation, and all physical existences conclude in a fall from beauty,
and life is as flickering and unsteady as a flash of lightning, one must therefore practice firm heedfulness.
Therefore, strive to increase your merits through generosity and the ornament of ethical conduct;
for for a world turning back toward the difficult path of birth, merits are the supreme foundation.
That the moon shines with its quality of luster, surpassing the splendor of the hosts of stars,
and that the thousand-rayed sun blazes, transcending all luminous bodies— that is the result of the excellence of one's meritorious qualities.

Ministers and kings of haughty nature, by the power of the merit of the lords of the earth, have their pride entirely subdued through the conduct of noble horses; as if filled with affection, they bear the yoke of his commands.
Misfortune follows those devoid of merit even as they strive upon the path of ethics;
for she, being rebuked by those of superior merit, turns toward their adversaries as if out of indignation.

Having desisted from that which is rooted in suffering, followed by infamy, and leading to the path of non-merit, set your minds upon the pursuit of merit— the auspicious means for the arising of happiness.
Having accepted his instruction with the words "So be it," and having saluted and circumambulated him, they each departed for their own dwellings.
Not long after those companions had gone, that Great-souled One fell into reflection:
"By whatever means possible, one must show honor to a guest who has arrived."
They possess the power to ordain this; I alone am the one to be pitied here.
These bitter sprouts of grass, severed by the tips of my teeth, cannot be given to a guest; fie upon this total lack of capability!
"Thus, for one so powerless and wretched, what purpose is there in my life? For whom such a guest has come to me, even Ānanda would turn to grief."
Then, reflecting, "Now that this worthless body is being cast off due to my failure in serving guests, for whose benefit might it be? that Great Being regained his mindfulness:
"Ah!
This blameless thing, so easily and independently obtained, belongs indeed to me alone."
The body and wealth are the means capable of honoring guests and people.
Why then do I despair?
I have obtained this hospitality; O heart, abandon your dejection and despondency. Since it has arrived, I shall honor the request of my guest with this very body.
Having thus resolved, that Great Being, having attained what was like a supreme gain, remained there with a mind of supreme joy. An extraordinary reflection unfolded within his heart;
it manifested both the power and the benevolence of the celestial dwellers.
Then, as if from joy, the earth with its mountains became tremulous, its garment of the oceans agitated;
the sound of celestial drums resounded in the sky, and the quarters of the horizon shone, adorned with clarity.
Clouds that laughed with incessant, low rumbling and were girded with lightning on all sides,
showered him continuously with flowers whose pollen was scattered by their mutual friction.
Carrying with him the fragrant pollen born of the flowers of various trees, the wind, moving with a steady course,
joyfully honored him as if with garments of fine cloth, their devotion undivided and increased by delight.

Having perceived that, while his marvelous resolve was being proclaimed on all sides by deities whose minds were filled with joy and wonder, and while his own mind was overflowing with astonishment and curiosity as he sought to understand the true nature of that Great Being,
on the second day, as the sun— possessing the power of exceedingly sharp rays— was ascending into the midst of the sky, its garments consisting of shimmering nets of light;

When the quarters of the sky were shrouded by the spreading radiance of the blazing sun and became unbearable to look upon; when the shadows in the forest depths were shrinking while the air resounded with the increasing cries of peacocks; when the flight of birds was interrupted and travelers had their vigor sapped by the fatigue of the heat—Śakra, the lord of the gods, assuming the form of a brahmin, appeared like a traveler who had lost his way, his throat distressed by hunger, thirst, exhaustion, and despair.
Weeping aloud, he cried out to them from nearby:
"I am one who has strayed from my caravan and am wandering in the dense forest; my body is exhausted by hunger and fatigue—worthy sirs, you ought to protect me! (AJm 6.22)

"Who here will gladden me with words of 'Do not fear,' as I wander alone in this wilderness, distressed by heat, thirst, and fatigue, my mind uncertain regarding the knowledge of what is the path and what is not, and utterly confused about the directions? (AJm 6.23)
Then those great beings, their hearts shaken by that sound of his most piteous wailing, approached that place with a hurried gait full of agitation.
Beholding him looking as miserable as a traveler who has lost his way on the road, they drew near and, after first offering words of courtesy, spoke to comfort him:
"Enough of your agitation; you have simply become lost in the wilderness."
For you remain close to us, as if you were among your own circle of disciples.
Therefore, O gentle one, having bestowed your favor upon us today by accepting our service, you shall depart tomorrow as you desire.
Then Udra, perceiving from his silence that the invitation was accepted, approached him with a hurried gait due to the agitation of joy; having brought seven rohita fish, he said to him:
"These seven fish—either forgotten by their enemies, or leaping onto dry land out of fear, or as if fallen asleep from exhaustion—have been found by me. Dwell here and eat them."
Then the jackal also, having brought him the various kinds of food he had found, spoke respectfully with a prostration:
"I discovered here a lizard and a vessel of curd abandoned by someone;
please use these out of consideration for my welfare, and may you dwell in this forest, O abode of virtue."
Having said this, with a joyful mind, he presented that to him.

Then the monkey, taking ripe mangoes that had become soft through the process of ripening— deep orange as if colored by red arsenic powder, with stems of deep crimson and gathered into clusters— spoke to him with palms joined in reverence:
"The mangoes are ripe, the water is delightful, and the shade is cool with the joy of meeting a virtuous friend."
Thus it is, O best among the knowers of Brahman; having eaten this, let your dwelling be right here with me.
Then the hare, having approached him and performed the customary rites of hospitality, gazed upon him with great respect and invited him to partake of his own body:
"There are no mung beans, no sesame seeds, and no rice for one who has grown up in the forest—what else could there be for a hare?
Let this body of mine, consecrated by fire, be consumed today; dwell then in this grove of asceticism."
Whatever wealth one possesses that serves as a means to achieve one's desires, one employs it in the festival of receiving supplicants;
and since I possess no wealth greater than my body, accept this, which is my entire possession.
Śakra said:
"How could one such as I even commit the slaughter of another?
What need is there for further discourse with one such as you, who has shown such benevolence?"
The hare said: "This is most fitting for a Brahmin who is near to compassion.
Therefore, may you remain right here out of regard for our favor, until I obtain some means of favoring myself from somewhere."

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, perceiving his intention, miraculously created a smokeless heap of embers, with the color of refined gold, emitting flickering, slender flames and scattering a profusion of sparks.
Then the hare, looking all around, saw that mass of fire;
having seen it, with a joyful mind, he said to Śakra:
"I have found this means for my own deliverance."
Therefore, you ought to fulfill my hope for favor by making [this gift] fruitful through its enjoyment by my body;
behold, O Great Brahmin!
There is the object to be given, a mind inclined toward the desire to give, and the union with a guest such as yourself.
For this cannot easily be attained; may it therefore become fruitful for me through my taking refuge in you.
Having thus conciliated him with respect and honor, and having greeted him with the affection one shows a guest, he—
like a seeker of wealth beholding a blazing treasure— suddenly ascended that flaming fire with supreme joy, as a lone swan enters a lake of blooming lotuses.

Seeing this, the Lord of the Gods, his mind overcome with supreme wonder, resumed his own form and, after honoring that Great Being with words pleasant to the mind and ear accompanied by a rain of celestial flowers, took him up himself with both hands— hands enriched with the beauty of lotus petals and adorned with radiant fingers and ornaments— and showed him to the deities.

Let the honorable gods dwelling in the abode of the thirty-three behold this; let them rejoice in this most wonderful deed and life-story of this Great Being. Alas! This one, out of affection for his guests, has today abandoned his body without attachment;
even those of unsteady nature are not capable of abandoning their bodies, which they regard like discarded flower offerings, without trembling.
Where is this birth, and where is this generosity that opposes it, along with such mental acuity? This is a clear repudiation by both gods and men of those who have little regard for merit.
"Oh, how his mind is perfumed by the practice of virtues!
Oh, how his affection for noble conduct is revealed through the magnanimity of his actions! (AJm 6.36)

Then Śakra, desiring to proclaim the excellence of that deed and out of regard for the welfare of the world, adorned the moon-disk upon the pinnacle of the excellent Vaijayanta palace and the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods with the mark of a hare’s image. Even today, this hare’s image remains complete within the moon.
Like a reflection in a mirror, it shines and radiates brilliantly.
From that time forth, the moon— whose laughter is the bed of night-lotuses and who is the tilaka-mark of the night— is celebrated by the world as Śaśāṅka (the One with the Hare).
Thus, since even great beings who have gone into the animal realm are seen to engage in the practice of giving according to their capacity,
what person existing in human form would not give?

Likewise, even those who have gone to the animal realm are honored by the virtuous out of affection for their qualities; thus, one should show respect toward virtues—this is how the point should be applied.
The sixth is the Śaśajātaka.
7. The Agastyajātakam:
Generosity and heroism are an ornament even for those dwelling in the forest of asceticism, let alone for householders.

Thus it is heard: while the Blessed One was still a bodhisattva, wandering upon the path of *saṃsāra* for the sake of the welfare of the world, he entered a certain great brahmin family that was distinguished by the purity of its conduct and virtues and served as an ornament to the surface of the earth— just as the stainless, full orb of the moon in autumn adorns the expanse of the sky.
The moon, as it were, adorned him as he rose;

having received in due order the sacraments such as the birth-rite prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, and having studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches, he pervaded the entire world of men with the fame of his learning, for he was requested by donors who loved virtue to accept wealth.
He attained supreme abundance of wealth;
with that prosperity, he gladdened his circle of kinsmen, friends, dependents, and the destitute, as well as his venerable guests and teachers, raining upon the lands like a great cloud.
His fame, already radiant through his learning, shone even more brightly because of his heroic generosity;
it was like the orb of the moon, pure in autumn, which possesses even greater luster due to its fullness.

Then that Great-souled One, having understood that the life of a householder is crowded with the faults of attachment to evil deeds, a source of negligence, agitated by the pursuit of acquiring and protecting wealth, opposed to tranquility, a target for hundreds of arrows of vice, a laborious engagement in endless occupations, productive of no satisfaction, and of meager flavor; and [having understood] that which is free from those defects, characterized by happiness, conducive to the practice of Dharma, and serves as the foundation for undertaking the Dharma of Liberation—

Beholding the greatness of the life of renunciation, he cast aside like a blade of grass that vast abundance of wealth— which had been acquired without hardship and was pleasing to the world through its universal esteem— and became devoted to the discipline and observances of the ascetic’s wandering life.

Even though he had gone forth as a wanderer, people seeking the highest good— whose minds were captivated by his multitude of virtues because of the radiance of his fame, their recollection of former associations, the estimation of his qualities, and the signs of his tranquility— [continued to follow him].
He likewise departed.
Disregarding that association with householders— which destroys the bliss of solitude and creates obstacles through attachment and distraction—
he, out of a love for seclusion, entered the midst of the southern ocean, which was as deep blue as a sapphire and tossed by the force of the wind.

By his mere presence, he endowed Kārādvīpa with the splendor of a hermitage; its shores were dappled by the playful movements of garlands of waves, its ground was strewn with white sand, it was graced by various trees whose branches were adorned with flowers, fruits, and sprouts, and it possessed the banks of a pool of pure water.
There, the one of beautiful form shone through his asceticism, while he himself became emaciated by that asceticism.
Like the new moon in the sky, he was slender yet not emaciated in his loveliness.
With his senses stilled by the practice of tranquility and dwelling in the forest, finding his sole delight in vows and restraints,
he was followed even by the deer and birds as "the Sage" because of their own feeble powers of intellect.

Then that Great-souled One, being accustomed to giving even while dwelling in the forest of asceticism, honored any guests who arrived at the proper time with whatever roots and fruits were available, with pure water, and with heart-pleasing words— gentle with greetings and blessings— and suitable for those engaged in penance.
And he sustained himself on forest-grown food, which was sufficient for his journey and consisted of the remains after guests had been served.

Śakra, the lord of the gods, his heart captivated by the fame spread abroad through the excellence of that one’s asceticism, desired to test the steadfastness of that Great Being; thus, in that forest retreat, he gradually caused all the roots and fruits suitable for the enjoyment of ascetics to vanish.

The Bodhisattva, too, because his mind was intent upon meditation, through his familiarity with contentment and lack of infatuation, and due to his lack of attachment to food or body, did not set his mind on the cause of their disappearance.
