Relying on the tender sprouts of trees to accomplish his need for food, he remained unsatiated by them, indifferent to superior kinds of food, and continued to dwell there with a healthy mind. For those whose selves are restrained by contentment, a livelihood is nowhere difficult to obtain.
Where, indeed, are grass, leaves, and pools of water not found?

But Śakra, the lord of the gods, his mind even more struck with wonder by that state of being and his conviction in the Bodhisattva’s exceedingly firm virtues, for the sake of testing him, caused the entire multitude of shrubs, grasses, and trees in that forest region of the wilderness to be stripped of their abundance of leaves, like the winds of the summer heat.

Then the Bodhisattva, having gathered very fresh withered leaves and subsisting upon them after steaming them in water, remained there with an undisturbed mind, his heart gladdened by the bliss of meditative concentration, as if satiated by the nectar of immortality.
For those who possess learning there is no pride; for those who are prosperous there is no envy.
And contentment is the supreme method for forest-dwellers to adorn themselves with virtue.

Then Śakra, his wonder greatly increased by that marvelous composure and steadfastness of the Great Being, as if filled with indignation, assumed the form of a brahmin and appeared before him like a guest— at a time when the Great Being had just completed his fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*), finished his recitation, and was looking toward the various directions in his desire to see visitors.
With a joyful mind, the Bodhisattva approached him and, preceded by kind words such as a welcome, invited him by announcing that it was mealtime.

Perceiving from his silence that the invitation was accepted, that Great-souled One— his beauty enhanced by eyes and face blooming with the excellence of his desire to give— welcomed him with affectionate words that were pleasing to the mind and ear.
Although it was obtained with great difficulty, he gave that entire cooked meal to him himself, and he became satisfied through sheer joy.
Having entered the meditation chamber in that very manner, he passed that day and night with that same joy and gladness.
Then, on his second and third day as well, Śakra appeared before him at the time of his vow in the same manner.
With a mind even more joyful, he likewise honored him;
for the desire to give in the virtuous increases through the practice of compassion.
He does not succumb to the wretchedness of contraction even by sufferings that end in death.

Then Śakra, his heart filled with supreme wonder, perceiving that through the excellence of his asceticism the king’s union with the splendor of the Lord of the Thirty-three would depend upon a mere request, became struck with fear and apprehension; assuming his own divine and wondrously beautiful form, he questioned him regarding the purpose of his asceticism:
"Having abandoned dear kinsmen with tearful faces, as well as possessions and the enjoyments of pleasure..."
Having cast away the goad of hope, where have you taken refuge in this affliction of asceticism?
Having disregarded the enjoyments of those born in happiness and having caused their kinsmen to suffer with grief,
the wise do not enter the penance groves that obstruct pleasure for the sake of a trivial cause.
If you think I should be told this, you ought to dispel our curiosity.
What indeed is it, by the mere report of whose virtues even your own intellect has been thus captivated?
The Bodhisattva said:
"Listen, friend, to the reason for this effort of mine:
birth again and again is exceedingly painful, as are old age, calamity, disease, and deformity."
And because of the agitation of the intellect that thinks "one must die," I remain here to protect the worlds from this [suffering].

Then Śakra, his heart comforted by the thought, "He does not desire the splendor belonging to us," and his mind further gladdened by that well-spoken word, honored those words of his, saying, "It is fitting," and invited the Bodhisattva with the granting of a boon.
"In this regard, O Kāśyapa, you who resemble an ascetic, I grant you a boon for these well-spoken words; choose whatever you desire."

Then the Bodhisattva, having no attachment to the pleasures of existence and perceiving even longing itself as suffering, being one whose contentment had become his very nature, said to Śakra: "If you wish to grant me a boon that brings favor, then I choose this boon from among those most excellent of the gods. (AJm 7.14)

May that fire of greed— which, even after obtaining wives desired by the mind, sons, sovereignty, and wealth more vast than one could hope for, still never brings satisfaction to a tormented intellect— never enter my heart.

Then Śakra, his mind even more thoroughly gladdened by that devotion to contentment manifested through the Bodhisattva’s well-spoken words, praised the Bodhisattva again, saying, "Excellent, excellent! and invited him to choose a boon:
"In this well-spoken discourse of yours, which is worthy of a sage..."
Out of affection, like a return gift, I grant you another boon.
Then the Bodhisattva, demonstrating once again the extreme rarity of freedom from the afflictions, taught him the Dharma under the guise of requesting a boon:
"If you grant me a boon, O Vāsava, abode of excellent virtues, then for that reason I choose this other boon, O Lord of Gods, which is not inferior. (AJm 7.17)
"Even through the mere appearance of their complexion, beings suffer ruin of wealth, fame, and happiness;
may that fire of hatred, by which they are overwhelmed as if by an enemy, remain far from me. (AJm 7.18)
Having heard this, Śakra, the lord of the gods, out of wonder, praised him with great respect, saying "Excellent!", and spoke again:
"It is only fitting that fame attends those who have gone forth as if out of affection;
therefore, accept this boon from me for this well-spoken word as well."
Then the Bodhisattva, out of aversion toward the afflictions, spoke as follows while censuring contact with afflicted beings under the pretext of choosing a boon:
"I would never even hear of a fool, nor would I look upon him, nor would I speak with him;
nor would I undergo the suffering of weariness from dwelling with him—this is the boon I choose from you."
Śakra said:
"Indeed, one who has fallen into misfortune deserves the special compassion of the virtuous;
for childhood is considered the lowest state because it is the root of all calamities."
Why, even though you are compassionate, do you not wish even to see this child, who is especially worthy of compassion?
The Bodhisattva said:
"Out of necessity, O noble one;
let your lordship look."
If it were possible to treat a fool in any way whatsoever, how could one like me remain effortless in the exertion for his welfare? (AJm 7.23)
Thus, let it be understood that he is unfit for the application of medical treatment:

he leads even others to ruin as if by sound policy; he desires to employ them here [in this task] despite their lack of fitness; and though addressed with what is beneficial, he becomes enraged because his conduct lacks the proper discipline and rectitude. (AJm 7.24)

Thus, when one is consumed by the delusion of pride in their own wisdom, and is harsh with anger even toward those who speak for their benefit; and when, out of a lack of application to discipline, they act with impetuosity—tell me, what means is there for bestowing benefit upon such a person?

Thus, O best of gods, even for those inclined toward compassion, there can be no granting of a sight— even if only a glance— to one who, due to his childhood, has become devoid of wealth, as there is no other recourse.
Having heard that, Śakra, greeting him with "Excellent! Excellent! and his mind delighted by these well-spoken words, spoke again:
"There is no price whatsoever for these jewels of well-spoken words;
however, out of affection, I grant you a boon here like a handful of flowers."
Then the Bodhisattva, demonstrating to Śakra the state of happiness found in every condition for a virtuous person, said to him:
"O Śakra, may I behold the steadfast one and may I hear the steadfast one;
O Best of Gods, grant me this boon: that my dwelling be with him, and that there be conversation with him."
Śakra said: "Indeed, you seem to show excessive partiality toward the wise man;
therefore, let it be told."
"What indeed has the Wise One done for you? Tell me the reason, Kāśyapa, why you, though yourself undiscerning, are so eager for a vision of the Wise One."
Then the Bodhisattva, demonstrating the greatness of this good man, said:
"Listen, sir, to why my mind desires only the company of the wise:
they walk themselves upon the path of virtue and lead others along that same path."
Even his speech, though not harsh, does not produce intolerance, for it is endowed with what is beneficial.

"He can always be made to accept what is beneficial through discipline that is free from deceit"—thus my mind, which is partial toward virtue, bows down before you, O you who are partial toward virtue. (AJm 7.31)

Then Śakra, rejoicing at this thought that his proposal was most appropriate, and with his faith further increased, invited him once more to choose a boon: "Since you are by nature contented, everything has already been accomplished for you; nevertheless, out of a desire to show me favor, you ought to accept a boon."
For one who has been approached with a disposition of service, devotion, and every possible effort, the non-acceptance of such a request is indeed a source of extreme suffering. (AJm 7.33)
Then, perceiving his supreme desire to be of service, the Bodhisattva, wishing for his pleasure and welfare, spoke to him while manifesting the intensity of his own longing to give:
"May your food be free from the defect of depletion, and may your mind be graced by the joy of the desire to give;
and may supplicants be adorned with pure virtue—this excellence of boons I choose. (AJm 7.34)
Śakra said:
"Truly, your honor is a mine of jewels of well-spoken words; moreover, everything that has been requested shall come to pass exactly so."
Furthermore, I grant you another boon for this well-spoken verse.

The Bodhisattva said: "O best of all celestial dwellers, if you would grant me a boon that brings about the perfection of favor, I choose this boon from you, the slayer of the Daityas: do not come near me again. Thus he spoke, blazing with intensity.
Then Śakra, filled with indignation and greatly amazed, said to him: "Wait a moment, sir!
By means of recitation, vows, sacrificial rites, and the labors of austerity, people seek to obtain a vision of me."
But for what reason do you not wish this, even though I have come before you desiring to grant a boon?
The Bodhisattva said:
"Enough of your insistence on anger;
I shall persuade His Majesty the King of the Gods."

For this lack of courtesy on your part is not due to a failure of devotion, nor is it an act of disrespect, nor do you desire to avoid meeting with me. Rather, having beheld your superhuman and wondrous form— radiant with a serene luster and blazing with splendor— I fear that you might become negligent in your asceticism, even though your appearance is so gentle and gracious.
Then Śakra, having bowed and circumambulated him, vanished right there.
When the night had turned to dawn, the Bodhisattva beheld an abundance of divine food and drink brought forth by Śakra’s power;
he also saw many hundreds of Pratyekabuddhas invited by Śakra, and numerous celestial youths with their girdles fastened tightly, ready to serve the meal.

By means of that method of providing food and drink, the sage, while fully satisfying the great seers, attained the highest joy; and he delighted in the conduct appropriate for ascetics, as well as in meditation, the immeasurables, self-restraint, and tranquility.

Thus, since even those dwelling in the forest of asceticism are adorned by the heroism of renunciation, let alone householders, a virtuous person should indeed adorn themselves with the heroism of renunciation. This [story] is to be applied to the praise of a lord of donors, to the censure of greed, hatred, and folly,
to the quality of associating with spiritual friends, to discourses on contentment, and likewise to the majesty of the Tathāgata— even in his previous births.
That Blessed One, the mine of the finest jewels of well-spoken verses, was already fully awakened even before this.
The seventh is the Agastyajātaka.
8. The Maitrībalajātakam:
Those possessed of great compassion, being afflicted by the suffering of others, do not look toward their own happiness.
Thus it is heard:

It is said that the Bodhisattva, whose resolute intention was to protect the world by means of his own majesty and compassion, became a king named Maitrībala. He grew ever greater through his preeminent virtues—such as generosity, self-control, restraint, and gentleness—which were conducive to the welfare of the world, and his mind was filled with loving-kindness toward all sentient beings.
Whatever suffering or happiness occurred among the subjects, that same experience befell the king as well;
therefore, being skillful in protecting his people, he took up both the sword and the treatises.

The weapon of him, whose edicts were worn upon the crest of the king of men, was like an ornament; and his treatise on statecraft was clearly seen to be for the sake of the world’s welfare and prosperity.
His engagement in both restraint and reward did not obstruct the Dharma,
because of his benevolent intention and skill in policy, like a discerning father toward his subjects.

While he was thus protecting his subjects according to the Dharma, and while he was increasing through the methods for accumulating the requisites of enlightenment— proceeding with ever more distinguished and noble stages by means of truthfulness, generosity, tranquility, wisdom, and other virtues dedicated to the welfare of others— once, on account of some offense, five *yakṣas* who were snatchers of vital energy (*ojas*), skilled in slaying enemies, were banished from their own domain by the lord of the *yakṣas*.
They arrived at that realm;

and having observed that the territory was endowed with supreme prosperity— characterized by constant and diverse festivals due to the absence of all calamities, and populated by people who were joyful, contented, and well-nourished— they [sapped] the vital energies of the men dwelling in that realm.
A desire arose in them to seize [the power] of these [beings]; though they exerted themselves with supreme effort in their own task,
they were simply unable to take away the vital energy (ojas) of those residing within that domain.
Because of the extraordinary power of that king, wherever his thought "this is mine" arose, that itself became his supreme protection; therefore, they were unable to steal away his vital energies.

And when, despite making even the greatest effort, they were unable to seize the vital energy (*ojas*) of anyone dwelling within that domain, they looked at one another and this thought occurred to them:
"What indeed is this, friends?
Are there perhaps special qualities consisting of the perfection of knowledge (*vidyā*) and asceticism (*tapas*), capable of counteracting our own power?"
Yet they do not exist; thus today we have all come to possess names that are rendered meaningless.
Then those yakṣas, having transformed themselves into the form of brahmins and following along,
saw a certain cowherd tending his cattle in the forest, sitting at the foot of a shady tree on a grassy plot, wearing sandals,
bearing a garland fashioned from the blossoms of wild trees with their sprouts, with his staff and axe laid down to his right, and alone, occupied with twisting ropes.
Approaching him as he sat singing with the playful grace of his warbling, they said to him:
"O you who are appointed to protect the cattle!
How is it that you do not fear wandering all alone in this forest, so secluded and devoid of human traffic?"
Looking at them, he said,
"Why should you be afraid?"
The yakṣas said:
"Have you not previously heard of the naturally fierce disposition of rākṣasas or piśācas? For even one who is accompanied by allies and endowed with knowledge, asceticism, and auspicious rites,"
From these, even a world that disregards fear through its own valor eventually attains liberation by some means.
How is it that you have no fear of those Rākṣasas who devour human fat and flesh,
while you are alone in the depths of the forest— solitary, profound, and terrifying?
When this was said, that cowherd laughed and said to them:
"This man is protected by a great benediction;
he cannot be overcome even by the lords of the gods, much less by flesh-eaters."
Therefore, even in the forest, I wander as if in a house; even at night, as if by day; and though alone, I move about without fear, as if in the midst of people.
Then those yakṣas, out of an intensity of curiosity, spoke to him with respect as if welcoming him:
"Tell us, tell us first, O blessed one, what kind of this particular rite for well-being is yours?"
Laughing, he said to them:
"Listen to the nature of our most wonderful and extraordinary rite for securing well-being.
[He is] one whose chest is as broad as a slab of the Golden Mountain, and whose face possesses the lovely splendor of the stainless autumn moon."
The lord of men had arms as thick and long as golden clubs, and his eyes and gait were like those of a bull.
"This is such a particular blessing for us," he said; then, looking at those yakṣas with indignation and astonishment, he spoke again:
"How wonderful!
How is it that the majesty of the king, so manifest as this, has not reached the path of your ears?"
Or perhaps, because it is so utterly marvelous, even though you have heard it, it has not taken root due to your disbelief.

I suspect that the people in this land are either incapable of seeking virtue, or they are devoid of curiosity, or perhaps they have abandoned the fame of the king due to the exhaustion of their merit; for such reasons you have come here.
There remains for you a residue of good fortune, in that you have come here from such a desolate wilderness.
The yakṣas said:
"Good sir, by what cause is this power of the king [such] that non-human beings are unable to harm the people living within his domain?
Gopālaka replied:
"This power of ours has been attained through the majesty of our great king;
behold it, O Brahmins!

His strength is loving-kindness (*maitrī*); his banner-top is variegated, yet his strength is merely his conduct. He knows neither anger nor harsh speech, and he protects the earth with perfect integrity."

For him, the Dharma is the method, not the deceit of worldly policy; wealth exists for the sake of honoring the virtuous. Thus, though filled with wonder, he does not resort to the riches or the pride of the wicked.
Our master is endowed with hundreds of such qualities;
therefore, calamities do not prevail against the people living within his domain.
Moreover, how much could I possibly say to you?

However, out of curiosity to hear of the king’s virtues, it would be more appropriate for you to enter the city itself; for there, your hearts will be captivated by the king’s qualities, as you behold a city where the noble boundaries of conduct are firmly established through devotion to one's own duty, which is ever-secure and well-supplied with food, joyful and prosperous, where the dress of its inhabitants is modest yet dignified, and which is exceptionally hospitable toward guests and visitors.
Seeing the people joyfully practicing praises based on his fame— as if they were performing auspicious rites and benedictions— they will infer the full extent of the king's virtues.
And when there is this manifestation of great respect for his virtues and a desire to see them, you will inevitably become direct perceivers of those qualities.

Then those yakṣas, because their own power had been thwarted, did not at all become softened by that truthful account of his virtues—however appropriate it was or how much it was applied with sincere intent—toward that king.
For generally, the minds of the dull-witted are inflamed by indignation; when a certain matter is praised, they burn with resentment toward that very person.
But observing the king's fondness for giving, those yakṣas, desiring to do him harm, approached the king at the time of his audience and asked for food.
Then that king, with a joyful mind, commanded the officials in charge:
"Let the food desired by the brahmins be given to them immediately."
Then those yakṣas did not accept even the food fit for a king that had been presented to them, just as tigers do not take green grass; they said, "We do not eat such food.
Hearing this, the king approached them and asked, "Then what kind of food is agreeable to you?"
"Search for such [food] as this. The yakṣas said:
"The flesh of humans while still warm, and their blood—this, O lotus-eyed one who has not broken his vow, is the food and drink of the yakṣas."

Having said this, they resumed their own bodies— bodies with mouths formidable with fangs, with fierce, squinting eyes that were glowing tawny, with flat and deformed noses, with hair and beards as tawny as blazing fire, resembling dark clouds laden with water, and distorted and terrifying.
Having observed them closely, the king reached the conclusion: "These are indeed piśācas and not humans; that is why they have no desire for our food and drink."
Then, in that king, whose nature was compassionate and whose mind was pure, an even greater compassion arose toward them.
With a heart single-mindedly intent on compassion, he felt pity for those yakṣas and reflected upon this matter:
"For one possessed of mercy, such food and drink are exceedingly difficult to obtain; and since they must be sought after every day, what indeed could be more painful than this? (AJm 8.18)
The exertion of one who is both merciless and powerless results solely in frustration;
what indeed could be more painful than that for one who possesses power yet practices what is harmful? (AJm 8.19)
When will the sufferings of those who are devoted to such food, whose minds are devoid of compassion and inauspicious, come to an end— both here and after death— as they burn away their own welfare?
Therefore, how could I now, by failing to provide them with food, cause even for a single day an obstruction to their request born of their desire to harm others?

For I do not recall ever having, out of selfish interest, made the faces of those who came seeking me as dejected as lotuses withered by the cold wind—their luster destroyed by the frustration of their hopes. (AJm 8.21)
"Let it be so; it has been seen.
From my own body, I shall give flesh that is firm and plump, along with blood. For when supplicants have arrived, what course of action other than this would be more appropriate for me? (AJm 8.22)
For the flesh of those who have died of their own accord becomes devoid of heat and bloodless;
nor are these dear to them, for their bodies are not truly afflicted by hunger.

Moreover, while I am still alive, from where else shall I obtain flesh? And how will these [beings], having approached me with their eyes and faces parched by hunger and thirst, depart with their minds even more afflicted by frustration because their hopes and entreaties have been rendered fruitless?
Therefore, this is the time for action here.
Like a malignant ulcer, this body is perpetually diseased and a source of suffering;
therefore, by applying myself to the performance of supreme duties, I shall endure the hardship of its treatment, which is exceedingly pleasant.

Having thus resolved, the king, his beauty of eyes and face expanded by an outburst of joy, showed them his own body and said to those yakṣas: "This flesh, along with its blood, has been preserved solely for the sake of the world's welfare. If they were to accept my hospitality today, that would be a great success and a source of prosperity for me."
Then those yakṣas, although they knew the king’s inner intention, did not believe it because of its extreme wonderfulness, and said to the king:
"When a petitioner has revealed the suffering within his soul through the wretchedness of his begging,
it is only the giver who ought to know what is appropriate for the occasion beyond this."
Then that king, his mind delighted at the thought, "This is their consent," gave the command: "Let the physicians be ordered to perform the venesection."

Then the ministers of that king, perceiving his resolve to give away his own flesh and blood, their hearts agitated by confusion and indignation, spoke these words out of affection regarding a certain matter: "It does not behove Your Majesty, in the impetuous haste of your joy at giving, to disregard the sequence of what is beneficial and harmful to your devoted subjects. Nor is this unknown to Your Majesty, namely—"
O giver of honor, whatever brings about the welfare of living beings is pleasing to the Rākṣasas;
O sinless one, it is the very nature of this race to find satisfaction in a livelihood acquired by obstructing others. (AJm 8.27)
O Lord, you who are unattached to pleasures maintain the glory of sovereignty solely for the sake of the world’s welfare;
therefore, abandon this resolve to give away your own flesh, which is a deviation from your own firm determination.

Without doubt, O hero among men, these people, protected by your prowess, cannot overcome the world; for, ruined by their expertise in harmful ends, they seek the ruin of the subjects through improper policy.
Through oblations poured into the sacrificial fires at rituals, the gods attain satisfaction by means of marrow, fat, and other such offerings;
yet it is said that your food, though purified by respectful treatment, does not at all please their palates.
Granted that Your Majesty’s intellect is not to be swayed by people such as myself, yet this devotion to your own interests causes you to fall so far from the path of proper conduct.
To deprive the entire world of its protector for the sake of these five—what kind of path of righteousness is this for Your Majesty?
Moreover:

"By what cause is there such a lack of affection toward us? Or by whom have our flesh and blood, which were previously hidden while being employed for the sake of our master, been revealed, so that Your Majesty desires to give away your own [limbs] even while these [servants] are not yet exhausted?"
Then that king said to those ministers:
"How could one such as I say that what exists does not exist, or clearly and discourteously say 'I will not give' when asked? (AJm 8.31)
If, while being the leader in the established order of Dharma, I were to myself walk along a wrong path, what would become of my subjects who follow the path of conduct practiced by me? (AJm 8.32)
Since I shall extract the very essence from my body by regarding only the welfare of living beings,
what power for accomplishing the world's purpose could there be for me, whose heart is small and seized by selfishness?
Furthermore, regarding that which you say with affection, great respect, and words imbued with love and confidence—
"For what reason do you show such lack of affection toward us, when Your Majesty desires to give his own flesh and blood while ours have not yet been exhausted?"— on this point I shall persuade you.
Indeed, my path of affection toward you is neither obstructed by the objects of your senses nor difficult to fathom due to a lack of trust;
rather, when wealth has gradually diminished or come to an end through the course of fate,
it is a friend whose affection expands who shines among those who are now poor, not one who was wealthy when they were destitute.
While my own limbs have grown large and are elevated with the accumulation of flesh for the sake of those who seek my wealth, it would be unseemly for me to show such affection toward you as well.
I would endure even the injury of those who are strangers; what need is there to mention you?
For it is my own flesh that I desire to give, and these people are begging for me, not for you.
Therefore, enough of this excessive affection and lack of fear regarding obstacles to the Dharma;
indeed, such conduct on the part of your honors for our sake is improper.
Furthermore, this matter ought first to be investigated.

How could one who wishes to give food and other gifts for his own sake be a person of virtuous conduct when forbidding another? How much less so when forbidding such a person from performing a meritorious act?
Therefore, enough of this persistence of yours in this matter.
Let your minds be restrained from the wrong path by an investigation according to reason, acting as our companions.
Indeed, your honors would shine with words appropriate to your approval; you should not appear thus with such agitated eyes. Why?
Every day, beggars do not come for wealth that has only a single use;
yet such a person seeking [wealth] cannot be found even by propitiating the gods.

When such a person seeking [his aid] has approached, even the path of reflection upon this perishable body—a mere abode of suffering—would be base; yet the wretchedness of stinginess is the ultimate darkness.
"Therefore, your honors ought not to prevent me," he said, thus conciliating them; then the king, having summoned his own assembly and had five veins lanced in his own body, spoke to those yakṣas:
"By accepting this body of mine, you ought to grant me assistance and supreme joy in my righteous deed."
Saying "So be it," they began to drink the king's blood— which was as copper-red as the juice of red sandalwood— with their hands joined in hollowed cups.
As his blood was being drunk by those night-stalkers, the lord of the earth shone with a golden body,
like Mount Meru embraced by clouds that are crimson at twilight and bowed down by the weight of water.
Due to the excellence of his joy, the perfection of his fortitude, and the very quality of that king’s body,
his limbs did not wither, his mind did not faint, and the flowing blood did not diminish.
But those Yakṣas, their thirst and fatigue subdued, said to the king, "This is sufficient."

Although the body— a constant source of manifold sufferings and ever ungrateful— had become for the lord of men a means for honoring supplicants, its being taken away occurred in a manner conducive to his joy.

Then that king, his eyes and face even more radiant with the awakening of great joy, took up a sharp sword whose blade was as pure blue as the petal of a blue lotus and whose hilt was beautiful and brilliant with the luster of jewels; having repeatedly cut off his own flesh,
he gave it to them.
But as his opportunity was being snatched away again and again by his joy in giving,
his mind could not endure to plunge into the pain of that severance.
As he was being drawn forward by the strikes of sharp weapons and pushed back again and again with affection,
his suffering became slow in its ascent toward the mind, as if due to exhaustion and lassitude.
Filled with joy, he likewise satisfied those night-stalkers with his own flesh;
by this means, even their cruel minds were revealed to have become softened.

Out of love for the Dharma or through the power of compassion, one who sacrifices their own dear body for the sake of others can transform even minds scorched by the fire of hatred into something fresh with the beauty of serene clarity.

Then those yakṣas, beholding the king intent on cutting out his own flesh, yet with a countenance as serene as before and unshaken by the pains of the incision, were filled with supreme faith and wonder. With their joy and reflection aroused, they exclaimed: "How marvelous! How extraordinary! Oh, what can this be? Is it real, or is it not?"
The kings, having suppressed their indignation, manifested a serenity of mind through praises and prostrations toward him.
"Enough, enough, O King! Desist from this course that brings suffering to your own body.

We have been fully satisfied by this most wonderful act of yours, which so captivates the hearts of supplicants. Having thus hurriedly and respectfully dissuaded the king, they stood with faces bathed in tears of joy.
Gazing up with great reverence, they spoke again:

"It is only fitting that people, under the sway of devotion, become eloquent in proclaiming your glory; it is only fitting that Fortune, abandoning the lotus grove, takes pride in seeking refuge with you.
Clearly, even though Heaven has Indra as its lord, it looks upon this earth—which is protected by your valor—with rising envy; otherwise, alas, it would be deceived."

What more need be said? Truly, this world of men is fortunate to be graced by the presence of such persons as you. Yet, we have been consumed here by our own remorse for having failed to rejoice in your exertions.
We ask [this] with the hope of counteracting our own misdeeds, thinking that even those who have come to such a state can rescue themselves by taking refuge in people like you.
Disregarding the royal splendor that has come to you so easily and is devoted to you,
what is this most extraordinary place that you desire by means of this path?
Do you perhaps desire through this asceticism the sovereignty over all the earth, or the status of the Lord of Wealth, or even the rank of Indra, the state of Brahmā, or final liberation?
For there is nothing more distant from this resolve than what you desire; if it is something we ought to hear, then you should speak it to us.

The King said: "Listen to the purpose for which this effort of mine is undertaken. Since that which is acquired through exertion perishes without effort, it cannot lead to the happiness of contentment, much less to peace.
Therefore, I do not desire prosperity based on worldly existence, even the glory of the Lord of the Gods, let alone any other."
Yet my mind does not proceed upon the path of contentment by means of the mere destruction of my own suffering,
when I behold these helpless embodied beings, afflicted by the exhaustion of intense calamities.
"By this merit, having attained all-seeing wisdom and having conquered the enemies that are the defilements,
may I rescue the world from the ocean of existence, which is agitated by the great waves of old age, sickness, and death."
Then those yakṣas, their hair standing on end with joy and devotion, bowed to the king and said:
"This deed is truly worthy of such extraordinary resolve.
Therefore, it is certain that the fulfillment of your intentions is not far off. Thus they addressed him with resolute minds.
Granted that this entire exertion of yours is indeed for the benefit of the world,
you ought nevertheless to remember us at that time, for there is this excessive concern for your own welfare.
"And for this reason that we have thus caused you distress out of ignorance,
failing to see even our own true interest— may you forgive us for that as well."
Furthermore, you ought to grant us your command with full confidence, as a path of favor, just as you would to your own ministers.
Then the king, perceiving that their hearts had been softened by his graciousness, said to them:

"This is indeed a favor to me and not a hardship; therefore, enough with this apprehension of my impatience. Moreover, having attained enlightenment, how could I forget such companions on the path of Dharma?"
I shall first grant you a share of the nectar of the Dharma of liberation.
Observing what is dear to us, you must avoid violence as you would poison;
likewise, greed for the possessions of others, censurable speech, and the sin of intoxication must be shunned.
Then those yakṣas, having promised him "So be it," bowed down, circumambulated him, and vanished right there.
At the very moment that Great Being resolved to give his own flesh and blood,
the earth, trembling in many ways, caused the Golden Mountain to quake violently.
The drums situated there resounded, and the trees shed their blossoms due to the earthquake.
Driven by the wind like a cloud in the sky, it was scattered everywhere around the king— spreading out like a flight of birds here, and in another place like a woven garland.

As if wishing to restrain the lord of the earth by the violent surge of its waves, the great ocean shone forth with waters whose natural roar was intensified, its body possessing the majestic luster of his departure.

"What is this? asked the Lord of the Gods, overcome with agitation; then, having reflected upon its cause and fearing the king’s demise, he hastened to the royal palace, which was utterly distraught by grief and terror.
But even for the Tathāgata, there arose a particularly great wonder at the graciousness of that king’s countenance;
approaching him, he praised that deed with pleasing words, moved by the power of his own serene joy.
Oh, the excellence of the conduct of the virtuous! Oh, the loftiness of the practice of virtue!
Oh, how exquisite is the mind intent on favoring others! Indeed, by being entrusted to you, the earth has found its protector.

Having thus praised him, Śakra, the lord of the gods, made his body free from pain and restored it to its former state using divine and human medicinal herbs capable of instantly healing wounds; then, having been honored by the king with a sweet reception of courtesy, humility, and service, he returned to his own abode.

Thus, since those of great compassion, being afflicted by the suffering of others, do not regard their own happiness, who indeed ought not to relinquish concern even for mere wealth? This should be said when exhorting donors, as well as when praising compassion, describing the majesty of the Tathāgata, or when listening to the Dharma with due reverence.
And as for what was said by the Blessed One, "These five monks are indeed very helpful," it was with this intention:
at that time, they were five yakṣas;
to them, the Blessed One first made a distribution of the nectar of the Dharma, exactly according to their vow.
The eighth [tale]: The Jātaka of Maitrībala.
9. The Jātaka of Viśvaṃtara:
It is not easy even for those of small capacity to rejoice in the conduct of a Bodhisattva, much less to practice it themselves.

As it is heard: Having made the conquest of his senses his very nature, having attained the glory of victory through excellence in prowess, policy, and discipline, and having realized the true meaning of the three Vedas and the science of inquiry (*anvīkṣikī*) by virtue of his constant attendance upon the elders, he was devoted to his own duties and rituals, surrounded by women who were accustomed to happiness and free from anxiety.

There was a king of the Śibis named Sañjaya, whose splendor of the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*) was manifested by his devoted subjects, and who had properly established the system of the economic pursuits (*vārttā*). The royal fortune dwelt with him, its affection bound by the emergence of his virtues, like a woman of noble family.
It was unassailable by other kings, like a cave protected by a lion is to deer.
Those who had exerted themselves in austerities, sciences, and arts, having come to his assembly,
received exceptional honor, their essential worth being manifested through various acts of worship.
Immediately after that king had assumed the sovereignty, he had a son named Viśvantara, who was the crown prince and was filled with a multitude of celebrated virtues;
at that time, he was none other than the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
Though young, he delighted in the tranquility of the aged; though radiant with splendor, his very nature was the bliss of patience.
Though learned, he was not intoxicated by the pride of knowledge; though enriched with prosperity, he was free from arrogance.

When the quarters had been traversed by him and the three worlds were pervaded by his glories, there was no longer even the slightest space or enthusiasm for the fragments of other men’s fame to spread.
Unable to endure the arrogance of those who cause the arising of suffering for the world, he—
raining down gifts with compassion as his great bow— seemed to enter into a state of martial fury against them.

Day after day, he greatly gladdened the seekers who approached him with the distribution of wealth— exceeding their desires, effortless, and made charming by the use of kind words and polite attentions. And on the festival days, adorned with the tranquility of the *poṣadha* vows and observances, having bathed his head and wearing white linen garments, he summoned a celebrated scent-elephant (*gandhahastin*) that resembled a peak of the Snowy Mountains, its face graced by a flow of ichor (*madalekhā*), and endowed with auspicious marks, discipline, speed, and strength.
Mounting his excellent state elephant, he inspected his own almshouses situated all around the city, which served as drinking wells for the needy;
and thus, he experienced a particular sense of joy.
For that prosperity which rests upon one's own home does not produce such joy for one who loves giving as that very same prosperity does when it is being transferred to the people who seek it.

Then, on one occasion, a certain neighboring king, having learned that such an instance of his [the Bodhisattva’s] generosity was being celebrated on all sides by supplicants with joyful hearts, reasoned thus: "He can be outwitted, for he has fallen under the sway of his passion for giving. With this thought, he dispatched brahmins there for the purpose of seizing his excellent elephant.

Then those brahmins stood before Viśvantara, who was inspecting his own sacrificial halls; their eyes and faces were more radiant with joy, they were vocal with blessings of victory, and they held their right hands raised and outstretched.
Restraining that excellent elephant, he asked them with due courtesy regarding the purpose of their visit: "Tell me, what is your need?"
The brahmins said:
"We have come to you because of your virtues and your heroic generosity, drawn by the grace of the gait of that serpent which moves with such languid elegance."
By the gift of this elephant, which resembles the peak of Mount Kailāsa,
cause the minds of the people to experience the singular flavor of wonder for a time.
When this was said, the Bodhisattva, his heart being filled with joy, fell into reflection:
"After a long time indeed, I behold suppliants with faces brightened by noble affection;
what need, however, have these brahmins for such a lordly elephant?"

"Clearly, this is a display of miserliness by some king whose mind is agitated by the defects of greed and envy. Let there not be such dejection from the frustration of hope for this monarch, who, disregarding both fame and dharma, has exerted himself as if for our own welfare."
Having thus resolved, that Great-souled One quickly descended from his excellent elephant and stood before them with a golden pitcher raised, saying, "Please accept this."

Then that wise man, though he knew that the treatises on statecraft had lost their path of righteousness through the pursuit of mere material gain, gave away the lordly elephant out of his love for dharma; he did not waver because of any deviation from ethical conduct.

Having given away that lordly elephant, adorned with beautiful ornaments of golden mesh like an autumnal mass of clouds wreathed in lightning, the prince attained supreme joy; yet the city was agitated by its partiality for the side of policy.
Then, upon hearing of the gift of the lordly elephant, the Śibis— the elder brahmins, ministers, warriors, and leading citizens— were stirred by a surge of anger and agitation;
raising a great clamor, they approached King Sañjaya and, with a mixture of haste, indignation, and fury, spoke to him while relaxing their formal decorum.
"O King, why is this royal fortune being thus destroyed while you remain indifferent? Your Majesty ought not to tolerate the ruin of your own kingdom as it continues to increase in this manner.
When they had spoken thus with agitation, the king asked them, "What is this? and they spoke to him again.

Why does the god not know? For he, having attended upon whose face—fragrant with the scent of rut and celebrated by the songs of intoxicated bees—the wind wipes away the prideful arrogance of rival elephants without the suffering of exertion. (AJm 9.12)
"By his splendor, the power and influence of your enemies have been eclipsed, as if their pride were fast asleep;
this elephant, given by Viśvantara, is your victory incarnate, being carried away to another land."

"O King, cows, gold, garments, and food are the forms of gifts to be given to the twice-born; but that upon which the glory of victory is certain—the lordly elephant—is what should truly be given. Such was his extraordinary generosity and valor.
"How will the royal fortune seek him out as he travels by this wrong path?
O King, it is not right for you to neglect this matter now, lest he should soon bring joy to your enemies."

Having heard that, the king—out of affection for his son, though somewhat displeased with them—said "So be it" with a sense of urgency due to the demands of state affairs; then, seeking to appease the Śibis, he spoke: "I know Viśvantara’s addiction to the practice of giving, which disregards the course of political expediency, yet this is not the proper way for one appointed to the burden of sovereignty. But as for the elephant he gave away, which was like his own vomit, who could possibly take it back?"
"However, I shall act in such a way that he will know the proper measure regarding giving;
therefore, enough of this agitation on your part."
The Śibis said:
"O Great King, Viśvantara cannot indeed be managed in this matter by mere words of reproach."
Saṃjaya said:
What else can I possibly do in this matter?
For one who has turned away from the pursuit of faults, the engagement with virtues is made into a source of calamity.
What could be the ransom for that elephant—his imprisonment or even his execution—for the sake of that son of one's own?
Therefore, enough of this agitation on your part;
I myself shall restrain Viśvantara from this.
Then the Śibis, their indignation aroused, said to the king:

"O lord of men, who would approve of the execution, imprisonment, or flogging of your son? For he is righteous by nature; because of his compassionate soul, he is not one to endure the agitation of the burden of kingship."
Those who have attained renown through their splendor and are skilled in pursuing the three aims of life resort to the lion throne;
but this man, because of his excessive devotion to dharma and his lack of regard for worldly eyes, is fit only to dwell in a forest of asceticism.
The faults of the wicked policies of kings bear fruit among those who depend upon them;
yet, even so, these are seen as endurable for the subjects because they do not obstruct the very root of the kings themselves.
What is the use of saying more on this matter? This is the firm resolve of the Śibis, who cannot endure your misfortune:
let the prince go to Mount Vaṅka, frequented by the Siddhas, for the furtherance of his asceticism.

Then that king, being addressed so harshly by those people who— out of affection, intimacy, and trust, and being intent on his welfare— pointed out the danger of this course, lowered his face in shame for fear of provoking public unrest; his heart overwhelmed with anxiety over the separation from his son,
he sighed wearily and said to the Śibis:
"If this is your insistence, then let him be excused for just one day and night;
at dawn, Viśvantara shall carry out what you desire.
When his conciliatory words were thus accepted by the Śibis with "So be it," the king spoke to his steward:
"Go and report this news to Viśvantara.

Having promised "So be it," his face drenched with tears of grief, he approached Viśvantara who had gone to his own palace; weeping aloud from the force of his sorrow and suffering, he fell at his feet.
When Viśvantara, inquiring with agitation, asked, "Is all well with the royal household?", the messenger, sinking down and faltering in his words and syllables, spoke to him.
"It is well for the royal family.

Then, being questioned again by Viśvantara, "Why are you so despondent? the chamberlain spoke slowly, his throat choked by a surge of tears and his syllables faltering and trembling due to his labored breathing: [He said: "O King, this is the very nature of worldly existence; it is not that I am lacking in affection. But having seen the suffering of others, my heart is pained. For the sake of all beings, O King, I beseech you: do not go to the forest."
O King, disregarding even your royal command which was full of conciliation, the undiplomatic Śibis,
being provoked to anger, have banished you from the kingdom.
Viśvantara said:
"What connection is there between my being exiled by the Śibis because they are angry? I do not delight in the path of misconduct, and I loathe negligence."
Where are my Śibis angry, since I do not see any misdeed?
The steward said:
"In your extreme generosity, your contentment was bright with selflessness, yet the minds of those who beg were agitated by greed."
O giver of honor, when that lordly elephant was given by you, your anger robbed the Śibis of their fortitude.
"Thus the impetuous Śibis have overstepped their own bounds because of you; go by that very path along which they have departed. (AJm 9.24)
Then the Bodhisattva, manifesting his own long-practiced compassion for supplicants and his excellence of supreme fortitude, said:
"The Śibis are indeed fickle by nature, as if ignorant of my own character.
What need is there to speak of external objects? I would give even my own eyes or my head."
For it is for the sake of this world that I bear this physical form; what indeed is the value of external things?
If one whose mind desires to honor even with his own limbs the words of supplicants should not give out of fear, that is considered a manifestation of childish caprice.
Moreover, you should speak thus to the Śibis on my behalf:

"I do not give this for the sake of fame, nor out of a desire for prosperity, O Śibis, nor out of greed. This path has not been followed by the base; I give simply because it is what ought to be given. (26)
"Let all the Śibis kill me or banish me as they wish; nevertheless, I will certainly not fail to give. I am going now to the forest of asceticism."
Then the Bodhisattva spoke to his wife, whose face was distressed by the hearing of unpleasant news: "Has your ladyship heard the resolution of the Śibis?"
Madrī said:
"O Lord, it has been heard."
Viśvantara said:
"Whatever wealth there is that you have obtained from us,
O lady of faultless limbs, deposit it here, along with whatever paternal wealth you possess."
Madrī said: "O Lord, where shall I place this?"
Viśvantara said:
One should always give gifts with honor to those who possess virtuous conduct;
for wealth thus bestowed is unseizable and follows one even beyond death.
Do what is pleasing to your parents-in-law, provide for the protection of your two sons, and remain diligent in your duty; however, do not grieve on account of my absence.
Having heard that, Madrī—though her heart was deeply distressed—disregarded her grief and despondency for the sake of preventing her husband’s loss of fortitude, and spoke thus:
"O Great King, it is not dharma that you should go to the forest alone;
therefore, O Kṣatriya, I too shall go by the same path as which you shall go."
For me, who am rolling in your lap, death would indeed be a festival;
yet more painful than death would it be if I were to live without you.

Indeed, O King, it does not even appear to me that dwelling in the forest is a hardship; for such is the case: the penance groves are more delightful than pleasure gardens, being free from wicked people, possessing rivers and trees yet untouched by others, resounding with the cries of various birds, teeming with deer, and featuring lawns as enchanting as floors of lapis lazuli.
Moreover, O King, beholding these two princes adorned and wearing garlands,
playing among the forest thickets, you will not remember the kingdom.
The ever-new beauties of the forest, fashioned by the seasonal efforts [of nature], and the river-groves filled with water will delight you in the woods. (AJm 9.35)
There was the wonderful singing and music of the birds longing for pleasure,
as well as the dances of the peacocks taught by their master, passion.
And the sweet, unblemished songs of the female bees,
performed as a concert in the forests, will gladden your heart.
And as the stone slabs were being spread with the silken garment of moonlight during the nights,
the forest breeze, having acquired its fragrance from the flowering trees, began to fan him.
The gentle splashing sounds of the river-brides, whose waters stumble over shifting stones,
will delight your mind in the forest like the tinkling of ornaments.
Thus being entreated by his beloved, he—his mind eager for the departure to the forest, yet out of regard for those who sought his aid—began to make a great gift.
Then, having learned of this news regarding Viśvantara’s exile, a tumultuous sound of lamentation arose within the royal palace.

Overwhelmed by the force of grief and suffering, the people seeking his favor fell as if into a swoon; like those intoxicated or insane, they wailed in many ways at the thought of those who had raised their axes for the purpose of cutting down the shade-tree that yielded sweet fruit.
That the earth, her nurse, feels no shame is clearly a sign of her lack of consciousness.
If there were no one to prevent those wishing to break into a watering place containing cool, pure, and sweet water, then alas,
the guardians of the world would either be useless in name only, or they would be far away, or their very existence would be a mere matter of hearsay.
"Alas, unrighteousness is awake, while righteousness is either asleep or dead, since King Viśvantara is being expelled from his own kingdom! (AJm 9.42)
Who is so skilled in causing misfortune, and so cruel in his intent to kill us—who are blameless and whose livelihood is not based on begging—as to exert himself against us? (AJm 9.43)

Then the Bodhisattva, having bestowed upon supplicants as was fitting all his treasuries and storehouses— numbering many hundreds of thousands— which were filled with jewels, gold, and silver, and contained various hoards of wealth and grain, as well as female and male slaves, vehicles, mounts, garments, and furnishings,
bowed down at the feet of his parents, whose fortitude was overcome by grief and sorrow, and departed together with his wife and children.
Having mounted his excellent chariot, he departed from the great city amidst the wailing of the vast multitude of people, as if it were the proclamation of a "Blessed Day.

Having with great effort turned back the following crowd—who were overcome by affection and whose faces were drenched with tears of grief—he himself took up the reins and set out toward Mount Vaṅka. With an undaunted mind, he passed through the vicinity of the great city, which was adorned with beautiful groves of pleasure gardens, and proceeded gradually toward the region where the trees provided sparse shade.

He reached the forest, where the flow of people was severed, which was crowded with herds of roaming deer, whose quarters were unobstructed by light, and which resounded with the chirping of jhillī birds.
Then, some brahmins who had arrived there by chance asked him for horses to draw their chariots.
While traveling on a journey of many yojanas, though he was without attendants and accompanied by his wife,
he gave four horses to the brahmins out of joy in making gifts, regardless of his future needs.

Then, as the Bodhisattva himself desired to take up the role of charioteer and was tightening his girdle with even greater firmness, four young yakṣas, appearing in the form of red deer, took up the chariot-pole themselves upon their shoulders like well-trained, noble horses.
Seeing them, the Bodhisattva said to Madrī, whose eyes were wide with joy and wonder:
"Behold the extraordinary power of these forests, honored by the presence of those whose wealth is asceticism;
for here, such affection for guests has taken deep root even among the noble deer."
Madrī said:
"I consider this superhuman power to be yours alone;
for even when the practice of virtue is firmly established, it is not always equal among the virtuous."
The splendor of the reflection of stars in the waters is especially enhanced by the blooming of night-lotuses;
here, the moon’s forefingers act as the cause, as if they have extended forth out of curiosity.
Thus, as they were traveling along the road, speaking kindly to one another out of mutual goodwill, another brahmin approached and requested the Bodhisattva’s excellent chariot.
Then, unattached to his own comfort and regarding the petitioner as a dear kinsman,
he fulfilled the brahmin’s desire with that chariot.

Then the Bodhisattva, with a joyful mind, descended from the chariot and, having handed over his own kinsmen, gave the excellent chariot to the brahmin; taking the prince Jālinī upon his hip, he set out on the road on foot alone.
And Madrī, her mind undisturbed, followed behind him, holding the young girl Kṛṣṇājinā upon her hip.
The trees, their branch-tips bent down by heart-pleasing fruits, seemed to invite him;
and, beholding him through the power of his merit, they bowed as if they were humble disciples.
And right there, wherever he desired water, lakes appeared with lotuses stirred by the shoulders of swans, their petals turned bright yellow-orange by the pollen of the filaments.
The clouds assumed the beauty of canopies, a pleasant and fragrant breeze blew,
and the Yakṣas, unable to endure the distress of his fatigue, shortened his path.

Thus the Bodhisattva, like one who has entered a pleasure grove, experienced the joy of strolling on foot; without tasting the weariness of the road, he reached Mount Vaṅka together with his wife and children. There, he beheld a place dense with various beautiful, glossy trees adorned with flowers, fruits, and sprouts, resounding with the diverse cries of birds intoxicated with joy, graced by flocks of peacocks engaged in dance, and frequented by many herds of deer—a place that seemed to have formed a protective enclosure around him with its pure, blue waters.

Having entered the penance grove—which was reddened by the pollen of flowers and cooled by pleasant breezes—and following the path pointed out by the forest-dwellers, he took up residence in a secluded leaf-hut.
This hut, built by Viśvakarman himself at the command of Śakra, was lovely to behold, pleasant in all seasons, and perfectly private.
In that forest, attended by his beloved wife and listening to the effortless, sweet prattle of his son, he dwelt.
As if dwelling in a garden, having forgotten all cares of sovereignty, he practiced austerities for more than half a year.

Then, on one occasion, while the princess had gone out for the sake of roots and fruits, and while the prince remained at the hermitage to ensure the protection of his two sons, a certain Brahmin arrived. His feet and shanks were made rough by the dust of the road; his eyes and face were withered by exhaustion; and he carried a water-pot suspended from his shoulder, bound upon a wooden staff, having come for the purpose of bringing a servant for his wife.
Having entrusted his firm message [to the messenger], he went to that place.

Then the Bodhisattva, seeing after a long time that a person seeking his aid had arrived, felt a surge of joy in his heart; with a serene expression on his face and eyes, he went out to meet him, welcomed him with kind words such as "Welcome," led him into the hermitage, and honored him as a guest.
He asked the purpose of his visit.
Then that brahmin, having cast aside his fortitude and shame out of affection for his wife, and being intent only on receiving a gift, spoke these words:
"Since there is light and the path is level, this world proceeds by that way and not by a difficult one."
But for the most part, in this world shrouded in the darkness of envy, no one else can bear my words of affection.

"By the glory of your fame, strengthened by the heroism of your giving, all that has been traversed and all that remains to be traversed have been accomplished. Therefore, I have come to you as a petitioner; grant me those two sons of yours to be my attendants."
When this was said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva—
who had practiced the joy of giving and was untrained in refusal—
boldly replied, "I give," even regarding his two beloved sons.
"May it be well!

Why do you sit there now? Thus addressed by the Brahmin, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, his heart held fast by the force of affection for his two sons whose eyes were overwhelmed with despair arising from hearing the account of the gift, spoke.
"These two have been given by me to you; however, their mother has gone to the forest for the sake of roots and fruits, and she will return this evening."
"Having seen my two sons, smelled their heads, and adorned them with garlands, you shall take them away tomorrow after they have rested here for one night. (AjĀ 9.57)
The Brahmin said: "Enough of this insistence on the part of your honor;
for it is established that the name 'vāmā' applied to women is merely figurative."
And if there should be an obstacle to your giving, for that reason I do not find staying here pleasing.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Enough with this fear of an obstacle to giving;
she is my partner in the practice of Dharma."
Or as it pleases your honor;
moreover, O Great Brahmin,
it is because of his delicacy, his youth, and his lack of skill in services.
What kind of devotion to you as a servant could these two possibly show?
But seeing that they had come to such a state, the grandfather, King Śibi, said: "Truly, I shall give you whatever wealth you desire as the ransom for these two."
Therefore, you ought to lead these two to that place;
for in this way, you will be united with great wealth and merit.
The Brahmin said:
"I shall not be able to approach the king, who is as difficult to assail as a venomous serpent, by means of an unpleasant gift;
for the king might seize these two from me, or he might inflict punishment upon me."
For this reason, I shall take these two as attendants for the brahmin woman.

Then the Bodhisattva, saying "Now as you wish" with his purpose yet unfulfilled, and having instructed his two sons with affectionate persuasion for the sake of accepting their service, tilted the water-pot over the outstretched hand of the brahmin;
by force of his effort, the water poured from the pot.
But with his own eyes, which were as copper-red as lotus petals, he himself—

Then that brahmin, his mind agitated by the excessive joy of his gain, spoke a blessing in hurried words and, with the harsh command "Depart!", began to drive the two princes out from the hermitage grounds.
Then the two princes, their hearts pained by the excessive burden of the sorrow of separation, bowed down to their father and, with eyes choked by tears, said:
"Mother has departed, O Father, and you wish to give us away;
let us first see her as well, and then Your Majesty may grant us."

Then that brahmin, reflecting that his mother might arrive before them or that remorse might arise in him out of affection for his sons, bound their hands with a creeper like a cluster of lotuses; threatening them, he dragged along those two princes, who were naturally delicate and struggling while turning their faces away from their father.
Then the young girl Kṛṣṇājinā, weeping aloud due to the onset of that previous suffering, said to her father:
"Father, this Brahmin beats me mercilessly with a creeper;
yet this man is clearly not a Brahmin, for it is said that Brahmins are righteous."
"This is surely a yakṣa in the guise of a brahmin who carries us away to devour us.
O father, why do you neglect us as we are being led off by this piśāca?"
Then Prince Jālī, grieving for his mother, said:
"This is not my sorrow that this twice-born man kills me;
rather, it is that I do not see my mother today which rends me as if apart."
Surely my poor mother will weep for a long time in the empty penance grove out of grief for her son, like a female cātaka bird whose chick has been killed.
"Having gathered much root and fruit from the forest for our sake,
how indeed will our mother fare upon seeing the penance grove empty?"
"Father, of these horses, elephants, and chariots that we have, half should be given to Mother; by this she will dispel her grief."
"O venerable one, by my word, you must prevent our mother from grieving in every way;
for, dear father, it is difficult indeed to behold her again."
"Come, Kṛṣṇā, let us die; what indeed is the use of life for the two of us?
We have been given by our parents to this Brahmin who desires wealth. (AJm 9.72)
Having spoken thus, they departed.
Then the Bodhisattva, although his mind was not shaken by that most piteous lamentation of his son, thought, "Who now, having given [this], would feel regret? Yet,
his heart being consumed by an inextinguishable fire of grief, his consciousness becoming obstructed as if overcome by the onset of a poison-induced faint, he sat down right there.

Having regained consciousness through the fanning of cool breezes, and beholding the hermitage as if silent and empty of his son, his throat choked with sobs and faltering, he spoke these words to himself:
"Alas, how could that shameless brahmin not have feared striking my very heart, which bears the name of my son, right before my eyes? Shame on him! (AJm 9.73)
Barefoot and shoeless, tender and unable to endure fatigue, how will those two travel the road, having fallen into the state of his servants?
"Who today will provide rest for those withered by the fatigue of the road? Or, struck by the suffering of hunger and thirst, whom shall they approach to beg? (AJm 9.75)
If even I must endure this suffering while seeking to maintain my fortitude,
what indeed will be the condition of those two sons of mine, who have grown up in happiness?
"Alas! The fire of separation from my son utterly consumes my mind;
yet, remembering the duty of the virtuous, who would indulge in remorse?"

Then Madrī, her spirits depressed by inauspicious omens foreboding the occurrence of some misfortune, though desiring to return as quickly as possible after gathering roots and fruits, reached the hermitage much later than intended because her path was obstructed by ferocious beasts.
Finding her two sons neither on the customary spot where they would have come to meet her nor in their usual play-grounds, she fell under the sway of intense grief.
Then, filled with agitation by this unwelcome and unexpected event, her eyes darting about in search of her son, she perceived that their calling was unanswered; distressed by grief, she lamented.

Just as it appeared to me before, when the forest resounded with the prattle of my children, that very same place now, due to the absence of those two, seems to me like a desolate wilderness, devoid of refuge. (9.79)
"Are those two princes perhaps asleep, overcome by the fatigue of their play? Or have they been lost in the dense forest?
Or, being dissatisfied because of my long absence, might they have hidden themselves somewhere out of childishness?"
And why do even these birds not cry out, if they too were agitated as witnesses to his slaughter?
Was he perhaps carried away by the exceedingly swift river, whose waves were like the surges of her unrestrained anger?
"May my vain and false conceptualizations not come to pass!
May it be well with the prince and his son!
May the ripening of these omens that portend what is undesirable fall upon my own body alone!"
What indeed is this? My heart seems to flee, its joy vanished without cause and shrouded by the darkness of despondency;
my limbs seem to dissolve, and the quarters of the sky seem to whirl in confusion.
"And this forest, its splendor ruined, seems to be reeling."

Then, having entered the hermitage and set aside the roots and fruits in a secluded spot, she approached her husband with due courtesy and asked, "Where are the two children? At that, the Bodhisattva, knowing the weakness of a mother’s heart through affection and the difficulty of announcing unpleasant news, was unable to say anything to her. For it is exceedingly difficult for one who is compassionate to approach a person worthy of kindness and inflict the mental anguish of the fire of unpleasant tidings. (AJm 9.82)

Then Madrī, concluding that it was clearly ill for her two sons since he remained thus silent in a state of grief and dejection, reflected as if with a distracted mind; not seeing her children anywhere in the hermitage grounds, she spoke again with a voice choked with tears:
"I do not see my two children, and you do not speak to me."
I am indeed destroyed, for a wretched woman does not speak what is unpleasant.
Having spoken thus, her heart overwhelmed by the fire of grief, she fell down like a creeper whose roots have been severed.
As she was falling, the Bodhisattva caught her, brought her to a bed of grass, and having sprinkled her with cool water, he spoke to comfort her once her life-breath had returned:
"Madri, I did not tell you of my sorrow all at once."
For steadfastness is not possible in a mind weakened by affection.
"A Brahmin, afflicted by the suffering of old age and poverty, approached me; I gave him two sons. Take heart, do not grieve. (AJm 9.85)
"Look at me, Madri; O Queen, do not lament for my two sons.
Do not strike my heart—as it were—with arrows—already pierced by the grief for my sons."
"How can it be possible not to give even one's life when asked?
Therefore, noble lady, rejoice in this gift of my son."

Having heard this, Madrī—her heart previously tormented by the fear of her sons' destruction, now with her grief diminished upon hearing news of her sons' survival—wiped her eyes to prevent her husband from losing his composure and, looking up at her husband with wonder, said:
"It is a marvel! What need is there for much more?"
Surely even the gods must have minds filled with wonder and speechlessness,
since envy finds no room to spread within your heart.
For thus, with the sounds of celestial drums spreading in all directions through their echoes,
the sky became filled with clearly articulated syllables and words out of its own reverence for the proclamation of your fame.
The earth, its breast-like mountain king trembling, seemed to shudder with intense agitation as if from intoxication;
and the sky became as if illuminated by lightning by means of the golden flowers falling from heaven.
Therefore, enough with this wretchedness of grief; having given [yourself], gladden your heart. Become once more a watering place for the world and a giver indeed.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, having become suspicious— thinking "What is this?"— when Sumeru, the king of mountains, trembled due to the shaking of the earth's surface,
learned from the world-protectors (Lokapālas), whose eyes were wide with wonder, that the cause of the earthquake was Viśvantara’s gift of his son;
with a mind reeling from joy and amazement, at the break of that night, he approached Viśvantara in the guise of a brahmin.
He approached him as if seeking a purpose.
Once he had been offered the hospitality due to a guest, he was invited by the Bodhisattva to state his need, and he asked for the Bodhisattva’s wife.
For the virtue of giving does not undergo exhaustion among the virtuous, just as water in great lakes never runs dry.
Therefore, I entreat you: you ought to grant us this wife of yours, who is like a goddess.
But the Bodhisattva, with an undisturbed mind, promised him, saying, "So be it.
Then, taking Madrī with his left hand and a water-pot with his right, he poured the water from the tip of his hand upon her; yet in the heart of the god of love, there fell instead the fire of grief.
Madrī was provoked to anger, yet she did not weep, for she understood his natural disposition;
though overwhelmed by the burden of unprecedented sorrow, she stood gazing at him as if painted in a picture.
Seeing this, Śakra, the lord of the gods, his heart overcome with supreme wonder, spoke in praise of that Great Being: "Aho!
How vast is the distance between the true and the false dharma!
What power do those of unrefined self have even to believe in such an act? (AJm 9.95)
While still not free from passion, one must give away even one's most beloved wife and children as if they were without attachment; what indeed is this exalted nobility?
Without doubt, as your fame is scattered in all directions by conversations devoted to your virtues,
other glories of renown will vanish before it, just as other lights disappear in the brilliance of the sun.
The Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Bhujagas, as well as the gods of the Thirty-three led by Vāsava, rejoice in this superhuman deed of yours.
Having spoken thus, Śakra assumed his own blazing form and, announcing himself, saying "I am Śakra," he said to the Bodhisattva:
"I give this Madrī, my wife, to you alone;
for the moonlight cannot remain apart from the cool-rayed moon."
"Even though she was given to the jackal, does she belong to him? She is indeed the wife of the lion; for the steadfast grant what they are asked for. (AJm 9.100)
The sprouts of the Victors maintain an even mind toward those who are superior, middling, or inferior;
therefore, they are honored in the world for this quality, and not because of their past actions.
Therefore, do not grieve over the separation from your two sons, nor fall into distress over the loss of the kingdom;
your father has returned together with them and will make the kingdom secure, having you as its protector.
Having spoken thus, Śakra vanished on the spot.
And through the power of Śakra, that brahmin brought the two sons of the Bodhisattva right to the realm of Śibi.
Then the Śibis, Sañjaya, and King Śibi [reflected upon] that most piteous and most difficult deed of the Bodhisattva.

Upon hearing this, their hearts were deeply moved; they ransomed the two sons of the Bodhisattva from the hands of the brahmins, and having appeased them and brought them back, they re-established Viśvantara in his very kingdom.
Thus, since the conduct of a bodhisattva is so exceedingly wonderful, one should neither show contempt nor harbor resentment toward those exceptional beings who are intent upon it;
rather, one should apply oneself to honoring the praises of the Tathāgata and listening to the Dharma with reverence.
The ninth is the Viśvantara-jātaka.
10. The Yajñajātakam:
Those with virtuous intentions do not submit to the deceptions of evil; therefore, one should strive for purity of intention.

Thus it is heard: the Bodhisattva, it is said, governed the earth that had come to him by succession of inheritance— a land brought to him by the power of his own merit, with all neighboring kings bowing in submission, free from thorns and rivals because of the pacification of disturbances such as those caused by foreign armies, and ruled under a single umbrella.
The lord of the earth, having conquered the enemies that are the senses, remained unattached to the fruits of enjoyment that are subject to reproach;
with his entire being dedicated to the welfare of his subjects, he made dharma his sole purpose and lived like a sage.
For he understood that the nature of the world is primarily characterized by imitation of the conduct of its leaders;
therefore, desiring to secure the highest good for his subjects, he applied himself especially to the ordinances of dharma.
He gave wealth, undertook the practice of ethical conduct, cultivated patience, and strove for the welfare of the world;
with a gentle appearance and a heart intent on the benefit of his subjects, he shone like Dharma incarnate.

Then once, although that realm was protected by his arms, due to the deficiency in the karma of sentient beings and because the sons of the gods who were in charge of the rain-making function had fallen under the sway of negligence,
a state of distress caused by drought broke out here and there.

Then that king, having reached the firm conclusion that "this calamity has clearly come upon me or my subjects due to a transgression of dharma," and being unable to endure their suffering because of his deeply rooted resolve for their welfare, questioned the elderly brahmins headed by the domestic priest as well as his ministers of counsel— all of whom were esteemed for their knowledge of the true nature of dharma— regarding the means to remove it.

Then, believing that the sacrificial ritual prescribed by the Vedas—which was terrifying due to its commencement involving the slaughter of hundreds of various living beings—would be the cause of abundant rain, they described it to him.
However, having learned of the matter, the king, because his nature was compassionate, did not inwardly welcome their words regarding the slaughter of animals ordained for sacrifice.
Out of deference to their conduct, he did not address them with harsh words of refusal, but instead set aside their discourse by shifting to another topic.

Furthermore, having found an opportunity through the introduction of a discourse on Dharma, they—unaware of the king’s profound and hidden intention—instructed him toward the performance of a sacrifice:

"The duties of kings which are fixed for the acquisition of the earth and its protection do not wait for their time; for you, O King, they must always be performed in their proper sequence, just as [the sequence] of Dharma and happiness."

How can your mind be so intent on negligence— like a loose rope— regarding him who is skilled in the pursuit of the three aims of life, who holds his bow for the sake of the welfare of his subjects, and who is the bridge to the world of the gods under the name of sacrifice?

O destroyer of enemies, this command of yours is honored by kings as if it were their own personal success; now is the time for you to perform sacrifices to gather those supreme blessings that blaze with fame.
Granted that you are always consecrated for sacrifice through your devotion to giving and your observance of religious vows, nevertheless,
it would be fitting for you to discharge your debt to the gods by means of rituals established in the Vedas.
"For when the deities are well-pleased by a successful sacrifice, they honor living beings with rain;
therefore, favor this sacrificial rite which brings welfare to your subjects and glory to yourself."
A thought arose in him:

"Alas, how poorly situated is this person who, possessing a fragile intellect easily led by the convictions of others, is neither an investigator nor a true lover of the Dharma, yet possesses mere faith; for indeed, those very ones who are esteemed in the worlds as worthy of refuge have themselves come to regard even violence as being in accordance with the Dharma."
Alas, people wander into the perilous straits of the miserable realms, following the evil paths ordained by him.
For what possible connection could there be between the slaughter of an animal and the dharma that leads to dwelling in the celestial realm or to the gratification of the deities?

"It is said that an animal being slaughtered goes to heaven by the power of mantras; therefore, its killing attains the status of dharma. This too is false, for who among others will receive [the merit] in the next world? (AJm 10.11)
