With a mind not turned away from unwholesome conduct and with no firm resolve toward auspicious deeds,
by what reason could a beast go to heaven— even if slaughtered in a sacrifice— without the refuge of its own past merit?
If one who has been sacrificed at a ritual were to go to the third heaven, then surely the twice-born would themselves become sacrificial animals;
since this rule is not observed anywhere, who indeed will accept their word?

Having abandoned the auspicious nectar of incomparable fragrance, miraculous power, flavor, and vitality held by the excellent Apsarases, the denizens of heaven will instead find joy in the slaughter of a pitiable beast for the sake of its fat and other such things. (AJm 10.14)

Having determined that this was the opportune moment, the king—as if eager for the commencement of a sacrifice—accepted their words and said to them: "I am indeed well-supported and favored, since your honors are thus so intent upon my welfare. Therefore, I desire to perform a thousand human sacrifices."
Let the ministers be instructed, according to their respective offices, to gather the necessary provisions suitable for that purpose.
Let a site suitable for the construction of a guest-house be examined, as well as the favorable lunar day, the karana, the muhurta, and the conjunction of the asterism appropriate for it.
Then the domestic priest said to him:
"O Great King, bathe now for the fulfillment of your desired aim at the concluding bath (avabhṛtha) of a single sacrifice;
thereafter, the commencement of the subsequent sacrifices will be made in due order."
For if thousands of human cattle were seized simultaneously, they would clearly lead to a state of distress for the subjects.
When the brahmins said, "This is so," the king replied to them: "Enough with your fear of provoking the subjects;
I shall make such arrangements that my people will not fall into distress."
Then that king, having assembled the people of the city and the countryside, said:
"I desire to sacrifice with a thousand human sacrifices (*puruṣamedha*). Yet, I am not able to appoint anyone who is unwilling or innocent to the state of being a sacrificial animal."

"Therefore, let this be known to you: from this day forward, whomever among you I shall behold— with my stainless eye of intelligence, which has shaken off the sleep of negligence— to be transgressing the bounds of moral conduct and defying my command, that person, a disgrace to his own family and a thorn in the side of the country, I shall seize for the sake of a sacrificial animal."
Then their most eminent members, with palms joined in reverence, said to him:
"O God among men, all the activities of your subjects are directed toward your welfare; what purpose, then, is served by this act of insulting them?
Even Brahmā ought to approve of your conduct; in matters concerning the standard of the virtuous, your honor is the ultimate authority."
Whatever is dear to Your Majesty is dear to us as well;
for nothing other than what is dear and beneficial to us is seen as dear to you.

Having thus accepted the words of the city-dwellers and country-folk, the king, with great public display and grandeur, dispatched trusted ministers to the countryside and the cities for the purpose of apprehending wicked people;
and he caused a proclamation to be made everywhere every day as follows:

The king, the giver of fearlessness, bestows safety upon the virtuous man whose wealth is his steadfast and pure conduct; yet he desires to sacrifice thousands of human-beasts for the sake of his subjects' welfare to those who delight in lack of discipline.

Therefore, whoever from now on, out of pride in following a life of unruly self-aggrandizement, disregards even the king’s command—which is honored by neighboring princes—shall be made a sacrificial animal by his own deeds; with his body bound to the sacrificial post, miserable with despair, he shall be seen by people as he withers away.
Then the people dwelling in that realm, observing the king’s diligent search for men of wicked character for the sake of sacrificial animals, hearing daily that most terrifying proclamation,
and seeing royal officers intent on seizing sinful persons arriving from all sides, abandoned their attachment to immorality and became devoted to undertaking the restraint of virtuous conduct.
Averse to the pursuit of enmity, favorably disposed toward mutual love and respect, with strife and disputes stilled, following the instructions of their elders,

skilled in sharing, hospitable to guests, and praising humility and modesty, they lived as if in the Kṛta Yuga; [driven] by fear of death, by concern for the next world, by family pride, and by a desire to protect their reputation.
And through the growth of a most pure disposition and a sense of shame, people came to possess the stainless ornament of their own virtuous conduct.

In whatever measure the people became devoted to the Dharma, in that same measure the guards especially sought out those of immoral conduct; and consequently, not a single person deviated from the Dharma.
Then, having heard this news concerning the events in his own country, the king— adorned with a special affection—
gratified his spies with extensive gifts for bringing such pleasant tidings and commanded his ministers.
My highest resolve was to protect my subjects, and they have now become worthy of my veneration;
furthermore, this wealth has been set aside for sacrifice, so that I may perform a rite according to my intention. (AJm 10.22)

"May whoever desires wealth as fuel for their happiness obtain it to their heart's content from my presence, so that this poverty which torments our realm may be banished to a land where it has no place. (AJm 10.23)
While I remain firm in my resolve to protect the people, and while the means for this task are augmented by an abundance of allies,
this suffering of the populace— kindling my indignation— seems to blaze again and again within my heart.

Then those ministers of the king, accepting his words with great respect, had alms-halls constructed in all the villages, cities, and market towns, as well as at rest-places along the roads; and as commanded by the king, they daily gratified those who came as supplicants with whatever objects they desired.
Then, having abandoned that poverty and simultaneously obtained wealth from the lord of the earth,
the people became adorned with various and manifold garments and ornaments, appearing as if the splendor of a vast festival had unfolded.
The king’s fame, expanded by the praises of joyful people, spread throughout all directions;
its extent increased like the pollen born from lotus filaments, which grows wider as it is carried by thin ripples.

Thus, as all the people turned toward virtuous conduct through the king’s reliance on the qualities of sound policy, the calamities—overpowered by the increase of merit—went to their destruction without remainder.
The seasons became pleasant due to their lack of imbalance, devoted to righteousness like new kings;
and the earth bore various crops, possessing lotus-filled and pure blue reservoirs of water.
Powerful diseases did not afflict people, medicinal herbs possessed their most potent virtues,
the wind blew according to the fixed laws of the seasons, and the planets moved along auspicious paths.
There was no fear caused by foreign armies, nor any arising from mutual conflict, nor any from divine calamities;
for while the people were devoted to the dharma of self-restraint and remained tranquil, it was as if the Kṛta Yuga had arrived there.

Now, when the king had thus pacified the sufferings of supplicants along with all calamities through this Dharma-sacrifice he had undertaken; when the earth was crowded with joyful people and delightful in its flourishing appearance; and while the world was occupied with reciting benedictions for the monarch and royal glory was spreading in every direction—a certain chief minister, his mind won over by the king’s gracious favor, spoke thus to the king:
Truly, this is well said:
"Because one constantly observes tasks that are superior, inferior, and middling, the cognitions of the Lord move ever higher above the [ordinary] cognitions. (AJm 10.31)

Thus, by means of this sacrifice of Dharma—which is free from the reproachable fault of slaughtering animals—the King has secured the welfare of his subjects in both worlds and pacified calamities as well as the sufferings of poverty. What need is there for more?
Fortunate indeed are those subjects!
The black antelope skin spread upon his body was like the crescent moon upon the person of the Night-Maker; his movements, naturally graceful, were not sluggish due to the constraints of initiation;

the beauty of the arrangement of hair on his head, which resembled a parasol, remained as it was; and by his acts of renunciation, he has stolen away even from the performer of a hundred sacrifices the wonder that rests upon his fame.
O knower of policy, the sacrifice of the world—which is generally attached to violence, miserable, and driven by the desire for rewards—is merely a sacrifice;
but for you, whose conduct is faultless and enchanting, sacrifice is the very ornament of your fame.
Oh, how great is the fortune of these subjects for whom you have become their protector!
For it is evident that even among subjects, a father would not be such a guardian.
Another said:

"People give what is called charity when wealth arises, being under the sway of hope for that; and even regarding virtuous conduct, one acts with a view toward social standing and having conceived a longing for heaven.
But this activity of yours, which proceeds out of a readiness to assist the affairs of others, is not observed among the ignorant, nor among those devoid of the application of spiritual essence."
Thus, those with virtuous intentions do not comply with the deceptions of evil; therefore, one should strive for purity of intention.
Thus, the exertion for the welfare of subjects brings about prosperity, fame, and happiness;
therefore, it is not possible for kings to conduct themselves by disregarding it.
The same should be stated regarding the instruction to a king:
"The practice of dharma brings prosperity to the subjects; therefore, one who desires prosperity must be a follower of dharma"—this too should be applied accordingly.

It must also be stated thus: "Violence toward sacrificial animals never leads to prosperity; rather, giving, self-restraint, and self-control lead to prosperity; therefore, one who seeks prosperity should be devoted to giving and the like."
"In this way, even in his previous births, that Blessed One’s mind was intent upon acting for the welfare of the world"—this should also be stated in the praise of the Tathāgata.
The tenth is the Yajña-jātaka.
The summary verse:
Vyāghrī, Śibi the lord of Kośala, the two merchants, and Śaśa likewise—
these were the givers of Agastya’s flesh and the experts in Viśvāmitra’s sacrifice.
The first chapter.
11. The Birth Story of Śakra:
Neither adversity nor the attainment of sovereign power causes the great-souled ones to slacken their compassion for sentient beings.

Thus it is heard: the Bodhisattva, having practiced meritorious deeds for no small length of time, having made generosity, self-restraint, self-control, and compassion his very nature, and being preeminent in his tireless activity for the benefit of others, once became Śakra, the lord of the gods.
The splendor of the Lord of the Gods shone forth even more intensely through its association with him, its power greatly augmented;
it was like the radiance of the moon clinging to a palace whose walls were freshly anointed with plaster and new cosmetic ointments.
That Lakṣmī, for whose sake the sons of Diti impetuously rushed forward and struck with their chests the mace-like tusks of the elephants of the quarters—
though she was brought to him by the happiness of the fullness of his fortune— did not make his heart stained with pride.

The hosts of Daityas, unable to endure his abundant fame— which had spread throughout all the worlds as a result of his perfect protection of heaven and earth— and his most wondrous prosperity, marched forth with a vast army consisting of elephants, chariots, horses, and infantry, made even more terrifying by the swelling pride of their imagination; its roar was as dreadful as the agitated ocean, and it was difficult to behold due to its blazing, stainless weapons and armor.

With their armies, they advanced against him for battle. Yet, although he was a man of dharma, his arrogance toward the enemy, the fear of the people— which is distasteful as it interrupts one's play— and his own majestic nature following the path of policy, gradually brought about a state of martial excitement in his heart.

Then that Great Being, having mounted his excellent golden chariot— which was yoked to a thousand choice horses, adorned with a beautiful banner bearing the insignia of the exalted robes, illuminated by the radiance of various jewels and gems, its body blazing forth, its two sides resplendent with various sharp and flaming weapons arranged in distinct rows, and covered with white woolen rugs— proceeded with a vast celestial army consisting of a variegated host of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
Surrounded [by his forces], he went forth to meet that army of asuras right at the edge of the seashore.
Then there commenced a battle that shattered the courage of the timid,
in which the armor of the combatants was mangled by the clashing of one another's weapons.
"Stay! Not so! Look here—where will you escape from me now? Strike! You shall not remain! Thus did they strike one another.
Then, as the tumultuous battle with its clashing weapons proceeded,
the sky seemed to burst forth with the sounds of kettledrums and the shouts of warriors.

When elephants, formidable like mountains tossed by the winds at the end of an eon, rushed at one another with insolence born from the scent of rut, and with indignation provoked by the act of giving;
Chariots with banners flickering like lightning spread out in every direction, their sharp rattling sounds resembling the ominous clouds of a portentous storm.
As the banners, parasols, weapons, armor,
and crowns of the heroic gods and dānavas were being cast down by their sharp, mutual arrows, [the battle raged].
Then, scorched by the arrows of the enemies of the gods, the army of the lord of the gods fled in fear;
but the lord of the gods alone stood firm in battle, holding back the force of his foes with his chariot.
Beholding the exceedingly fierce asura host— driven by excessive pride, with loud shouts, war-cries, and lion-like roars as they charged forward—
and perceiving his own army intent on flight, Mātali, the charioteer of the Lord of the Gods,
realized that the time for retreat had arrived and turned back the chariot of the sovereign of the gods.
Then Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saw the nests of Garuḍas situated upon a silk-cotton tree (śālmali) in the path of impact ahead of the pole of the ascending chariot.
As soon as he saw them, his heart was seized with compassion, and he spoke thus to Mātali, the charioteer:
"The bird-nests, crowded with fledglings whose wings have not yet grown, are sheltered within the branches of the silk-cotton trees."
"Drive my chariot in such a way that these [trees] do not fall, crushed by the chariot-pole."
Mātali said:
"O noble sir, these Daityas are indeed advancing against us."
Śakra said:
"What then?
Avoid them, avoid these nests of Garuḍas thoroughly!"
Then Mātali spoke to him again:
"O lotus-eyed one, by turning back this chariot, only the welfare of the birds would be secured;
for this army of our enemies, having finally found its opportunity among the gods, is indeed charging at us."
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, revealing his own extraordinary resolve and superior nature through the power of compassion, said:

"Therefore, turn back the chariot! Death by the blows of the terrible mace hurled by the lord of the Daityas is better for me—whose fame has been consumed by the cry of 'Fie!'—than life obtained by killing these beings whose faces are dejected with fear."
Then Mātali, having replied "So be it," turned back his chariot yoked with a thousand horses for him.
But the enemies, their prowess witnessed in battle, seeing that the chariot had turned back,
fled in haste, stumbling from fear, like dark clouds driven by the wind.

Even when his own army has been broken, one who returns and blocks the path of the enemy host restrains their arrogance and pride simply by virtue of being considered capable of valor, even if he is alone.
But having seen that asuric host broken, the army of the lord of the gods also retreated;
for there was no longer any affection among the enemies of the gods to turn back, since they were fleeing in fear.

Then the Lord of the Gods, being honored in the assembly by the thirty deities with feelings of both joy and shame, returned slowly from the field of battle to his city, his beautiful body radiant with the splendor of victory, while his inner apartments were filled with eager anticipation.
Thus, that very thing became his victory in battle.
Therefore it is said:
"The base man, devoid of compassion, commits evil; but even when encountering calamity, the man of mediocre intellect remains possessed of compassion."
But even at the risk of losing one's life, a virtuous person is no more able to transgress his own conduct than the ocean is able to overstep its shore.
Thus, having even sacrificed his own life and his sovereignty over the gods, the Blessed One has for a long time protected sentient beings.
Therefore, it is not fitting for a wise person here to feel even resentment toward them, let alone act wrongly; thus, one should be compassionate toward living beings as a noble one.
For this reason, the verse "Dharma indeed protects the one who practices dharma" should also be applied here.
Likewise, [it consists of] paying honor to the praise of the Tathāgata and listening to the Dharma with reverence.
The eleventh, the Śakra-jātaka.
12. The Brāhmaṇa Jātaka:
By their own sense of shame alone, virtuous persons do not transgress the boundary of proper conduct.
Thus it is heard:
the Bodhisattva, it is said, took birth in a great Brahmin family that was blameless in lineage and conduct, renowned for its adherence to its own dharma, and praised for its disciplined behavior.

Having received the purificatory rites in due order—namely, conception, the rite for a male fetus, the parting of the hair, and the birth ceremony—he dwelt with a teacher who was endowed with learning, noble birth, and proper conduct, for the purpose of studying the Vedas.
His proficiency in hearing, grasping, and retaining [the teachings], his devotion, his lineage, and the discipline established in his own family— these,
along with his composure adorned by tranquility even in youth, made his teacher’s face bright with affection and grace toward him.
For the mantras of subjugation are indeed always unimpeded qualities;
they work even for those scorched by the fire of hatred, let alone for those whose minds are healthy.
Then, his teacher, for the purpose of testing the character of all his disciples, frequently described during the intervals between their recitations the sufferings of his own poverty:

"Alas for this poverty, which is fruitless in its desires; it makes one wretched even among one's own kin, leaving no one to cry out for help, and joyless even at a festival; it is dull when the talk turns to giving. (AJm 12.3)
Poverty is a source of humiliation, a locus of exhaustion, and utterly devoid of happiness;
it is exceedingly weak, always sorrowful like a calamity, and truly most terrible.

Then those disciples, like well-bred horses urged by a goad, being moved by a sense of urgency born from their affection for their teacher, brought forth alms that were both more abundant and more excellent.
He said to them:
"Enough of this exertion on your parts."

The offerings of alms do not dispel anyone’s exhaustion born of poverty; rather, it would be more appropriate for you, who cannot endure our suffering, to exert this very effort toward the acquisition of wealth. Why?
Because food removes hunger, water removes thirst, mantra-speech removes poison, and medicine removes disease.
But the wealth gained by propitiating one's lineage destroys the suffering of poverty.

The disciples said: "What shall we do, O unfortunate ones, since our exertion of power is so limited? Moreover, O Preceptor, even if wealth were to be obtained like alms, we ourselves could not endure such suffering from poverty as this."
For the acquisition of wealth by Brahmins has poverty as its only means of receiving gifts;
yet this person is no giver—thus, being without recourse, we are ruined.
The teacher said:
"There are indeed other means of acquiring wealth for Brahmins prescribed in the scriptures;
however, our capacity having been sapped by old age, we are unfit for their practice."
The disciples said:
"O Preceptor, our prowess has not been impaired by old age. Therefore, if you consider us capable of undertaking those means prescribed in the scriptures, let them be told."
"We shall go so that we may discharge our debt for the labor of teaching you."
The teacher said:
"Even for the young, such means of acquiring wealth are indeed difficult to accomplish when their hearts are lax in resolve.
However, if there is this persistence on your part, then listen well: which one among the methods of acquiring wealth shall it be?"
In times of distress, theft is permitted for the twice-born; indeed, the ultimate state of distress in this world is poverty.
Therefore, one may take what belongs to others when it is not seen by them; yet all of this remains the property of the Brahmins alone.
Granted, those such as you would certainly have the power to seize wealth even by force;
however, this is not the proper course, for one's own reputation must be protected. Therefore, one should resolve thus regarding empty places.
Thus, with their restraints loosened, those disciples—except for the Bodhisattva—listened to his words as if they were reasonable, even though they were improper.
For, being naturally virtuous, he could not bring himself to approve of that;
yet, as they proceeded to act as if it were their duty, he suddenly spoke out to them.
But the Bodhisattva, with his face bowed down by shame, sighed softly and remained silent.

Then that teacher, observing the Bodhisattva neither approving of nor rejecting that method, and having conceived an appreciation for his virtues, thought regarding that Great Being: "Could it be that he does not acknowledge my theft because of a lack of resolve or perhaps a lack of affection for me?"
Then, having given rise to the reflection, "Is it perhaps out of a sense of duty? he spoke to the Bodhisattva in order to clarify its true nature:
"O Great Brahmin!
These twice-born ones, unable to endure my misfortune, have taken refuge in the path of heroic men."
But you appear dull-witted from a lack of resolve; surely you do not suffer at our misfortune.
"Even though my own suffering has been fully revealed by me in words, its extent unhidden, how is it that you remain as if composed, with a mind so steady and free from agitation? (AJm 12.12)
Then the Bodhisattva, with agitation, saluted his preceptor and said:
"May evil be averted!

It is certainly not because of a lack of affection or a hard heart that I remain thus, unpained by the sufferings of my guru; rather, it is because of the impossibility of the course shown by my preceptor."
For it is not possible to commit a sin anywhere while remaining unseen;
why?
Because privacy is impossible.
There is no such thing as privacy in this world for one who performs an evil deed;
for surely the spirits see those humans who are themselves unseen.
The sages, who have perfected their souls and possess the eyes opened by divine vision, do not see them; thus, the fool, conceiving himself to be in secret, proceeds toward evil.
But I, moreover, do not see anything that is empty, nor anywhere at all;
even that wherein I do not see another—surely that is non-empty by me alone.
Whether a misdeed is seen by another or committed by oneself,
that which is seen by oneself is the most clearly perceived.
One whose mind is distracted by one's own affairs may or may not observe the conduct of another;
however, one who applies a one-pointed mind to passion certainly knows when committing evil oneself.
"Therefore, for this reason, I remain in such a state.
Then the Bodhisattva, perceiving that his preceptor’s mind was completely pacified, spoke again:
"My mind has not reached a firm conviction that you would deceive me in this way merely for the sake of wealth."
Having understood this, who indeed would disregard the distinction between virtue and vice, and reduce the suppression of virtue to the price of wealth?
Indeed, I shall declare my own intention:
it would have been better for me to take a skull, clad in tattered rags, and gaze upon the prosperity of my enemy’s home;
yet, having cast aside shame even at the destruction of Dharma, my mind was not directed toward the position of the Lord of the Gods.
Then his preceptor, his heart overwhelmed with joy and wonder, rose from his seat, embraced him, and said:
"Excellent, excellent, my son!
Excellent, O great brahmin!"
This is worthy of you, Medhāvaka, who are adorned with tranquility:
that upon encountering any sign whatsoever, fools abandon the path of their own dharma;
yet the virtuous, whose wealth consists of austerity, learning, and knowledge, do not undergo transformation even in the face of supreme distress.
By you, your own stainless lineage has been adorned, as the sky is by the autumnal moon rising aloft;
your learning, renowned for its excellent conduct, has become meaningful, and my labor has borne fruit through the arising of happiness.
Thus, because of their own sense of shame (*hrī*), virtuous persons do not transgress the boundary of proper conduct; therefore, one should become a noble person endowed with the power of shame.

This should be applied to such scriptural passages as: "The noble disciple, being thus endowed with the moat of shame, abandons the unwholesome," and so forth, as well as to those discourses connected with the praise of shame and those concerning the sovereignty over the world.
The twelfth Jātaka, the Brāhmaṇa-jātaka.
13. The Story of Unmādayantī:
Even for those virtuous beings afflicted by intense suffering, there is no inclination toward base paths due to their reliance on their own fortitude.
Thus it is heard:

once, it is said, the Bodhisattva, striving for the welfare of the world through his preeminent virtues such as truthfulness, renunciation, tranquility, and wisdom, became the king of the Śibis; he was like the Dharma itself, like the Vinaya, and like a father to his subjects, ever intent on their benefit.
Restrained from the pursuit of vice and established in the nobility of virtue by that king,
as if by a father toward his son, the people rejoiced in both worlds.
For his policy of governance was impartial toward both his own kin and other people, following the path of Dharma;
by closing off the unrighteous path for the people, it became like a flight of stairs leading to heaven.
Perceiving the lineage of the Dharma that benefits the world, that protector of the human realm, whose sole purpose was that very end,
devoted himself with his whole being to the path of Dharma and could not endure its suppression by others.

And that king had a daughter, the chief of the citizens, who was like Śrī incarnate, like Rati herself, or like one of the foremost of the Apsarases; endowed with the supreme perfection of beauty and charm, she was most beautiful to behold and esteemed as a jewel among women—
she remained so until her form became visible to the eyes of people who were not yet free from passion.
For that long, he was unable to move his gaze, which was bound by her beauty and virtues.
And for this reason, her kinsmen gave her the name Unmādayantī.
Then her father sent word to the king:
"O King, a jewel among women has appeared in your realm; therefore, Your Majesty is the authority regarding whether she shall be accepted or dismissed."
Then that king commanded the brahmins who were experts in the marks of women:
"Let your honors examine her to see whether she is suitable for us or not."
Then her father, having led those brahmins into his own residence, said to Unmādayantī,
"My dear girl, serve the brahmins yourself.
Having assented with "So be it," she began to serve the brahmins in due order.
Then those brahmins,
their eyes fixed motionlessly upon her face, their fortitude being carried away by the god of love,
became powerless over their own eyes and minds; they were as if robbed of consciousness by intoxication.
And when they were no longer able to remain steady and composed through their analytical discernment, much less to eat,
the householder removed his daughter from their sight and, serving the brahmins himself, dismissed them.

Then the thought occurred to them: "Truly, this is like a magical illusion; how exceedingly captivating is the beauty and grace of this girl! For it is not even fit for the king to look upon her, much less to take her as his wife.

For by the splendor of her form, his heart will surely become infatuated, and with his enthusiasm for the pursuit of dharma and worldly affairs dissolving, he will neglect the timing of royal duties, thereby obstructing the path to the welfare and happiness of his subjects."
Pressing him hard, they would bring about his defeat;
for she, by her mere appearance, could cause an obstacle to the success of even the sages,
let alone that of a young king who dwells in pleasure and whose gaze is fixed upon objects of passion.
Therefore, perceiving that this was the opportune moment, they approached the king as the occasion required and reported:

"Your Majesty, we have seen that maiden. While she possesses a certain beauty and grace, she is nonetheless disfigured by inauspicious marks and devoid of splendor; therefore, Your Majesty ought not even to look upon her, much less take her as your wife."
For a woman who brings reproach upon both families eclipses their fame and prosperity,
just as a cloudy night with a submerged moon obscures the beauty and the distinction between heaven and earth.
Having heard this matter, the king thought, "She is indeed ill-favored and not suitable for my family," and thus his desire for her ceased.
But perceiving the king's lack of interest, that householder gave the girl to the king’s minister, Abhipāraga.

Then, on one occasion, that king—his mind eager to behold the Kaumudī festival, which had come in due course and whose splendor was concentrated within his excellent city—mounted a choice chariot and set out. The city’s streets and marketplaces were sprinkled and swept; umbrellas, banners, and flags were raised on all sides;

the ground was variegated with offerings of flowers; dancing, singing, laughter, rhythmic movements, and instrumental music were underway; and a sweet fragrance spread abroad from the scent of flowers, incense, aromatic powders, perfumes, garlands, spirits, bathing unguents, and ointments.

Wandering through that preeminent city, whose royal highways were crowded with citizens dressed in exceptionally bright attire and who were contented and well-fed, and where various beautiful wares were displayed for sale,

he approached the residence of that minister. At that moment, she— Unmadañjanī— though she was actually ill-omened and had been rejected by the king as such, felt a surge of indignation, yet was simultaneously driven by a curiosity to see the king.
Her beauty of form being clearly visible, she stood illuminating the palace roof like lightning upon the peak of a cloud;
let her now have the power to maintain her composure, for her memory was shaken by the sight of those ill-omened signs.
Then, the king's gaze, which had been wandering over the splendors of the ornamentation of that preeminent city, suddenly fell upon her as she stood before him.
Thereupon, although the king’s eyes were already captivated by the graceful charms of the beauties of the inner apartments, he gazed at her with intense longing.
He was not arrogant, yet through his devotion to the path of Dharma, he was diligent even in the conquest of the senses.
Though possessed of the quality of vast fortitude and feeling a sense of shame, and though his eyes were usually averse to gazing at another’s young wife,
he— his heart stirred by the wonder of rising passion— beheld that woman for a long time with unblinking eyes.
"Is this Kaumudī herself, or perhaps the tutelary deity of this palace? Is she a celestial woman or a daughter of the Daityas? For this form is certainly not human."
Even as the king was reflecting thus, his eyes unsatiated by the sight of her, the chariot passed beyond that place and no longer followed the course of his desire.

Then the king, as if with a vacant heart yet with a mind one-pointedly fixed upon her, returned to his own palace; there, his fortitude shaken by the god of love, he questioned the charioteer Sunanda in private:
"Whose house is that, surrounded by white walls, which you know?"
Who was it that shone there, like a flash of lightning amidst a white cloud?
The charioteer said:
"There is a minister of the king named Abhipāraga; that house belongs to him, and she is his wife, Unmādayantī by name, who has a daughter named Kirīṭavatī.

Having heard this, the king’s heart became despondent because she was another's wife; with eyes motionless from anxiety, he sighed long and hot, and with his mind fixed upon her, he slowly spoke these words to himself:

Oh, how the name of this girl of pure smiles has been fashioned, with its syllables so charming and soft in accordance with their meaning! For indeed, it has made me as if intoxicated by her who is called "Unmādayantī" (the Intoxicating One).
I wish to forget her, yet I seem to see her with my mind;
indeed, my heart remains fixed upon her, as if she were there by her very power.
"Since another man’s wife is [the object of my desire], such lack of self-control belongs to me as well;
therefore, like one who is insane, I have today been abandoned by sleep as if by shame."

As my mind was rendered motionless by passion at the sight of her graceful form, smiles, and glances, the *nālikā*— suddenly resounding with a bold sound that announced the sequence of other duties— pierced my heart with resentment.

Thus, that king, his fortitude shaken by the power of passion, even as he sought to steady himself, became one whose body was pale and thin, intent on brooding, sighing, and yawning; the signs of love became manifest, for that transformation of the monarch’s mind, though concealed by great self-restraint,
revealed itself through a face with eyes fixed in thought and through his emaciation.

Then a minister, whose intellect was skilled in discerning gestures and outward appearances and who was well-versed in statecraft, having learned of that incident from the king along with its cause, feared for his safety out of affection; yet, knowing the overwhelming power of passion, he approached the king in private once he was aware of the matter, and having received permission, he addressed him thus: "Your Majesty, it is known that the daughter of King Brahmadatta has been seen by you. She is of such beauty that even the gods would be captivated by her; how much more so, then, a mortal? For this reason, O Lord of the Earth, you should not disregard her, lest she fall into the hands of some base person. Moreover, Your Majesty, the king of Kāśī is exceedingly powerful; therefore, you should take her as your queen-consort and bring her here. Thus he informed the king. The king, being delighted, agreed to his proposal. Then the minister, having obtained the king's consent, went to King Brahmadatta and spoke these words: "O King, your daughter has been seen by our lord. She is of such beauty that even the gods would be captivated by her; how much more so, then, a mortal? Therefore, let her be given to him; let there be an alliance between us. King Brahmadatta, being pleased, gave his daughter to the king of Videha. The king of Videha, having taken her, returned to his own city. There, he took her as his queen-consort and lived happily with her. Thus ends the story of the daughter of King Brahmadatta. Now, another story follows. Once upon a time, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there lived a king named Śatānīka. He was virtuous, wise, and beloved by his subjects. One day, while wandering through the city, he saw a certain woman of great beauty. She was like a goddess descended to earth, captivating the eyes and hearts of all who beheld her. The king, struck by her beauty, was overcome with desire. He sent messengers to inquire about her identity, but they could find no one who knew her. The king, however, remained obsessed with her, unable to forget her. He became pale and wasted away, neglecting his royal duties. His ministers, seeing his condition, were filled with concern. One among them, a wise counselor, realized the cause of the king’s distress. Fearing for the king’s life due to his deep affection, and knowing the immense power of love, he approached the king in secret. Having been granted leave, he spoke to him: "Sire, why do you suffer thus? Who is this woman who has stolen your heart? If she be a human, seek her out; if she be divine, pray to the gods for her sake. Do not let your mind be so troubled; for the mind of a king should always be steady. The king, hearing these words, sighed deeply and said: "Friend, she is no mere mortal; she is surely a celestial nymph. How can I obtain her? Yet, my heart is fixed on her alone; I cannot live without her. The minister, understanding the depth of his passion, reflected: "This king is truly devoted to dharma, yet he is now enslaved by lust. I must act so that he may attain his desire without violating righteousness. Having thus resolved, he devised a plan. He summoned a courtesan of great beauty and skill, and instructed her: "Go to the king and serve him with all your art. Win his favor so that he may grant you whatever you desire. The courtesan, accepting the task, went to the palace and began to attend upon the king. By her charm, grace, and clever conversation, she gradually won his heart. One day, when the king was in high spirits, she said to him: "My lord, if you are pleased with me, grant me a boon. The king, charmed by her, replied: "Ask anything you wish; I shall grant it to you. The courtesan said: "If it be so, then grant me this: that I may dwell in your inner apartments as your queen. The king, being bound by his word, agreed. She entered the harem and lived there, enjoying every luxury. Through her influence, she managed to have the king’s attention turned toward her. In time, she became his favorite. Thus, by the minister’s wisdom, the king attained his desire without losing his honor. This is the end of the story of the minister’s ingenuity. Now, another tale follows. Once, in the city of Mithilā, there was a king named Janaka. He was a great devotee of Viṣṇu and a patron of the learned. One day, a wandering ascetic arrived at his court. He was a master of logic and debate, and he challenged the king to a discussion on the nature of the soul. The king accepted the challenge and engaged in debate with the ascetic. After many days of argument, the ascetic was defeated. The king, pleased with his victory, offered him a reward. The ascetic said: "O King, I am a seeker of truth, not of wealth. Grant me this: that you grant me an audience whenever I wish, and that you listen to my teachings with respect. The king agreed. From then on, the ascetic came regularly to the palace and instructed the king in spiritual matters. The king, following his advice, practiced self-restraint and devotion. Thus, through the ascetic’s guidance, the king attained peace of mind. This is the end of the story of King Janaka and the ascetic. Now, another story follows. Once, in the city of Ayodhyā, there was a king named Daśaratha. He had three sons: Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Bharata. Rāma was the eldest and most beloved. One day, the sage Viśvāmitra arrived at the court seeking protection against demons. The king, honoring him, promised to send Rāma with him. However, Kaikeyī, the king’s second wife, remembered two boons previously granted to her by the king. She demanded that Rāma be exiled for fourteen years and that her son Bharata be installed as heir apparent. The king, bound by his promise, was forced to agree. Rāma, though grieving, obeyed his father’s command and departed for the forest with Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā. During their exile, they faced many trials, including the abduction of Sītā by Rāvaṇa. Ultimately, Rāma slew Rāvaṇa and recovered Sītā. He returned to Ayodhyā and was consecrated as king. Thus ends the story of Rāma and Sītā. Now, another story follows. Once, in the city of Hastināpura, there was a king named Dhṛtarāṣṭra. He was blind but possessed great wisdom. His son was Duryodhana, who was wicked and jealous of his cousins, the Pāṇḍavas. The Pāṇḍavas, led by Yudhiṣṭhira, were virtuous and brave. One day, a great gambling match was held. Duryodhana, instigated by Śakuni, cheated Yudhiṣṭhira at dice. As a result, the Pāṇḍavas lost their kingdom, their wealth, and even their wife, Draupadī. They were forced to go into exile for twelve years, followed by one year of living incognito. During their exile, they met many sages and heroes, including Bhīmasena, Arjuna, Nakula, and Sahadeva. Finally, after fulfilling the conditions of their exile, they returned to battle. A great war ensued between the Kauravas and the Pāṇḍavas. Arjuna, with the help of Kṛṣṇa, slew Duryodhana and his army. Yudhiṣṭhira was then crowned king. Thus ends the story of the Mahābhārata. Now, another story follows. Once, in the city of Kauśāmbī, there was a king named Udayana. He was handsome, wealthy, and beloved by his subjects. One day, a beautiful maiden named Vāsavadattā arrived at his court. She was the daughter of a merchant. The king, seeing her beauty, desired her. He sent messengers to ask for her hand, but the merchant refused, saying: "She is already betrothed to another. The king, disappointed, remained sorrowful. His ministers advised him: "Sire, do not despair. We shall find a way to win her. They devised a plan. They disguised themselves as merchants and traveled to the merchant’s city. There, they met the merchant and said: "We have heard of your daughter’s beauty and would like to see her. The merchant, thinking them to be honest men, invited them to his house. When they saw Vāsavadattā, they were struck by her beauty. They praised her virtues and said: "She is indeed a jewel among women. The merchant, pleased, said: "If you truly admire her, I shall give her to you. The king’s agents, having secured her, brought her back to Kauśāmbī. The king married her and lived happily with her

"O lotus-eyed one, today as you were worshipping the gods in person, O lord of men, a yakṣa approached me and said: 'Why do you not know that the heart of the king is fixed upon Unmādayantī? (AJm 13.17)
Having spoken thus, the discerning one suddenly vanished; such is what I have understood.
If that is indeed so, O King, why do you maintain this silence toward us, as if devoid of affection?
"Therefore, O Lord, it behoves you to accept her for the sake of showing me favor.

Then the king, his face bowed with shame at the refusal, though subject to the power of passion, remained firm in his composure because of his long-practiced sense of dharma, and replied to him in clear words of rejection:
"This is not so. Why?"
May I fall from my merit and not remain immortal; may even common people know of this sin of ours.
And through the fever of separation from you, that fire shall consume you as it once did a forest thicket.

Whatever action brings harm to both worlds—both in this life and in the next—is that for which the ignorant devote themselves, but for that very same reason the wise do not devote themselves. (AJm 13.20)
Abhipāraga said:
"Enough of your fear regarding a transgression of dharma in this matter;
by providing assistance in this gift, it will surely become dharma for you."
On the other hand, by not accepting her from me, there would be unrighteousness due to the obstacle to giving.
Furthermore, I see no occasion here for Your Majesty’s reputation to be impaired. Why?
For who else besides the two of us would be capable of knowing this?
Therefore, do not harbor suspicion in your mind out of fear of public scandal. (AJm 13.22)
"And this would be a favor to me, not a hardship. Why?
Because when the mind is filled with constant satisfaction earned through service to my master, what obstacle could there be?
Therefore, O Lord, fulfill my desire; enough of your suspicion that you will cause me pain. (AJm_13.23)
The king said: "May this evil be averted!
Clearly, out of excessive affection for us, you did not consider this;
for in every act of giving, providing assistance is not always the means for accomplishing dharma."
"Is she not indeed the wife of that friend, distinguished among kinsmen, who out of excessive affection for my sake does not regard even his own life?"
Therefore, it is improper for you to deceive me in this matter.
Even as for what was intended—that no one else would know of this—how could such a thing be sinless?
For even if one commits a sin while remaining unseen, how could one attain peace, just as one who consumes poison?
Neither the gods with their pure vision nor the yogis among men fail to see him.
Moreover,
who would believe this— that she is not dear to you,
or that by abandoning her immediately you would not meet with disaster? (13.27)
Abhipāraga said:
"With my wife and children, I am your slave; you are my master and my deity.
Since I shall give her to you, O Lord, what transgression of dharma is there for you?"
And as for what you have said—"She is dear to me"—what of it?
O granter of desires, she is indeed dear to me; for that very reason, I wish to give her to you.
For by giving what is dear, one obtains in the next world dear things that are exceedingly beautiful.
"Therefore, let the god indeed accept her."
The king said: "Do not say so! This is out of order. Why?"
I would indeed rather enter a sharpened weapon or a fire of blazing flames than, having attained prosperity through righteousness, strike at that very same righteousness again.
Abhipāraga said:
"If Your Majesty does not wish to accept her on the grounds that she is my wife, then I shall prescribe for her the profession of a courtesan, which is contrary to the requests of all people;
then, O King, may Your Majesty accept her."
The king said:
"Are you mad?
By abandoning a blameless wife, you would incur punishment from me."
Having become an object of reproach, you shall be consumed both in this world and in the next.
Therefore, enough with this persistence in what should not be done;
be one who is devoted to the right method.
Abhipāraga said:
"If there should be any transgression of dharma on my part, such as public scandal or the ruin of happiness,
I shall meet each of those with my chest, using instead the mental joy obtained from your own happiness."
O great lord of the earth, I see no one else in this world superior to you as an Āhavanīya fire;
please accept me, who am maddening with love, for the increase of my merit, just as a priest accepts a sacrificial fee.
The king said: "Granted, out of excessive affection for me, you have disregarded the sequence of what is beneficial and harmful to yourself in this exertion of service for my sake.
For that very reason, however, I ought not to neglect you specifically.
Indeed, you must not be one who has no fear of public censure. Behold:"
He who disregards the censure of the world, being indifferent to dharma or to rewards from others, no one places trust in him; moreover, he is utterly forsaken by prosperity.
Therefore I say this to you:
let not the transgression of Dharma appeal to you, even for the sake of life;
for it is a certain great evil, whereas the gain [of life] is uncertain and meager.
Furthermore:
Having cast others into the sufferings of blame and the like, the virtuous do not seek the attainment of their own happiness.
Therefore, I shall remain established in Dharma and undertake the burden of my own true welfare, even if I must do so alone, without afflicting others.
Abhipāraga said:

"As I act for the sake of my master out of devotion, what possible opportunity for unrighteousness could there be in this? Or rather, what unrighteousness would there be for Your Majesty in accepting her as she is being given, such that the Śibis, together with the merchants and the people of the countryside, would say, 'In this there is unrighteousness'?"
"O God, may you indeed accept her."
The king said:
"Truly, your mind is inclined toward acting for my sake;
however, this must be considered here."
"Among the Naigamas, the people of the countryside, and the Śibis, who among us—whether you, me, or anyone else—is the most learned in the Dharma?"

Then Abhipāraga, with great agitation, said to the king: "O King, because of your diligent application to the service of the aged, your mastery of sacred learning, and the sharpness of your intellect,
the ultimate truth regarding the three aims of life and the sciences resides in you as much as it does in Bṛhaspati."
The king said: "Therefore, you ought not to deceive me in this matter. Why?
Because the welfare and the harm of the world depend upon the conduct of kings.
Therefore, having reflected upon the devotion of my subjects, I shall delight only in the path of the righteous, which is conducive to fame."
Just as cows follow after the bull’s movement, whether it be crooked or straight,
so too do subjects follow the conduct of the king, free from apprehension and without the jolting of the goad.
Moreover, let Your Honor consider this:
if I do not even have the power to protect myself,
what state would be that of a person who desires protection from me?
Thus, beholding the welfare of my subjects, as well as my own stainless duty and fame, I do not wish to yield to the power of my mind; for I am the leader of my subjects, like a bull.
Then the minister Abhipāraga, his mind gladdened by that state of the king, bowed to the monarch with palms joined in reverence and said:
"Oh, what a perfection of supreme fortune for the subjects, O god among men, that you yourself are their protector!
For such devotion to Dharma, regardless of personal pleasure, is indeed to be sought even among those dwelling in the forests of asceticism."
"O Great King, this title 'Great' shines forth only upon you; for to apply the word 'virtuous' to those devoid of virtue is indeed an expression of words even more harsh than contempt."
What cause for wonder or agitation is there in this for me regarding you,
since you are a mine of virtues, like the ocean is of jewels?

Thus, even for those afflicted by intense suffering, there arises an absence of inclination toward the base path due to their reliance on their own fortitude and their well-practiced perception of the Dharma; therefore, one should apply oneself to both fortitude and the practice of the Dharma.
The Thirteenth Jātaka: Unmādayantī.
14. The Supāraga Jātaka:
Even the truthful word that takes refuge in the Dharma dispels calamity, let alone its fruit; therefore, one should be a follower of the Dharma.
Thus it is heard:
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, possessed of supreme and subtle intelligence, was once a helmsman.

For this is the natural law of Bodhisattvas, due to their innate wisdom: that whatever exceptional treatise they wish to investigate, or whatever specialized art, they become preeminent and wise in each and every one of them.
Of the world.

Then that Great Being, because he understood the movements of the stars, was undeluded regarding the divisions of the directions; he was thoroughly conversant with the fixed and adventitious omens of portents; he was skilled in the sequence of proper and improper times; he had well-identified regions of the ocean by means of signs such as fish, water-colors, types of ground, birds, and mountains; he possessed mindfulness, had conquered sloth and sleep, was patient with the exhaustion of cold, heat, rain, and other hardships, was vigilant, steadfast, and, due to his skill in advancing and retreating, was capable of his task.
He was one who brought merchants to their desired destination;
because his voyages were always most successful, he came to be known by the name Supāraga,
and the city where he resided became famous as Supāraga itself.
That which is now known as Śūrpāraka.
Because he was considered exceedingly auspicious, even in his old age, he was placed upon the ship by sea-faring merchants desiring the success of their voyage, preceded by entreaties and honors.
Then once, some merchants desiring success on their journey set out from Bharukaccha for Suvarṇabhūmi; having reached the port of Supāraga, they entreated that Great Being to board their ship.
He said to them:
When my vision is being withdrawn by the command of old age, when my memory is diminished by the onset of exhaustion,
and when my strength has failed even in the tasks of my own body— what kind of assistance can be expected from me?
The merchants said:
"This condition of your bodies is known to us.
Even though you possess the capacity for great exertion, we do not wish to weary you by assigning you labor. What then?"
"By being honored through taking refuge in the lotus of your feet, this boat of ours has attained auspiciousness;
thus, we have come to you so that it may sail safely even across this great and difficult ocean. (AJm 14.2)
Then that Great Being, out of compassion for them, boarded that vessel even though his body was weakened by old age.

Upon his boarding, all those merchants became joyful in heart, thinking, "Surely our supreme success in the voyage is certain. And in due course, they entered the ocean, which was frequented by various schools of fish, filled with the unrestrained clamor of water, and where the waves were tossed about by the play of the wind.

[He beheld] the great ocean, its surface adorned with various jewels and precious gems, variegated by garlands of foam-flowers, the abode of the foremost asuras and the best of serpents, possessing an inaccessible bottom and immeasurable waters;
it was as intensely blue as a mass of sapphires, appearing as if the sky had melted from the heat of the sun’s rays.
They went into the midst of the deep ocean, where the line of the shore had completely vanished from all sides.
When they had arrived there at the time of evening, while the sun’s power of its circle of rays had grown soft, a great and most terrifying portent appeared.
With waves breaking and foam scattered about, and with a fearsome roar from the lashing of fierce winds,
the ocean suddenly became violent, its entire body of water abandoning its tranquility.
With vast masses of water and land tossed by calamitous winds and whirling with terrifying force,
the ocean assumed a formidable form, like the earth itself trembling at the end of an eon.
Clouds, with flickering tongues flashing like streaks of lightning and resembling many-headed blue serpents,
veiled the path of the sun, resounding with continuous and terrifying peals of thunder.
With its web of rays shrouded by dense, thick clouds, the sun gradually ascended toward the setting;
the darkness, having gained full scope at the end of the day, seemed to reach a state of solidification on all sides.
In the great ocean, whose circle of waves was drenched by showers of arrows, the ship trembled excessively as if rising up in rage;
it shook as if terrified, filling their hearts with despair.

Trembling with fear, silenced by despair, yet steadfast and agitated in their search for a remedy, they were intent on supplicating their own deities; thus they manifested their various states according to the quality of their respective natures.

Then those seafarers, their ship being tossed about by the force of the wind and the current, did not see any shore even after many days, nor did they see the familiar signs of the ocean as they had desired; rather, with their despondency increasing due to entirely unprecedented signs of the sea, they fell into a state of agitation caused by fear and despair.
Then the Bodhisattva Supāraga, steadying them, said:
"Indeed, for those who have plunged into the ocean, the distress caused by sudden storms is no marvel. Therefore, enough with your continued despondency."
Despair is not the method for remedying misfortune; therefore, enough with embracing dejection.
For those who are skilled in undertaking action through fortitude cross over hardships without difficulty.
Therefore, having cast off despondency and wretchedness, devote yourselves to action with the opportunity for duty;
for the splendor of a wise man, kindled by fortitude, is the very hand that grasps the attainment of all goals.

Thus, those merchants, their minds steadied by that Great Being and their thoughts eager to see the shore, gazed upon the ocean and beheld beings in human form, appearing like men clad in silver armor, repeatedly rising and sinking.
Having carefully observed their appearance and characteristics, they reported it to Supāraga with great wonder.
"Indeed, this unprecedented sign is observed here in the ocean:
these are surely Daitya warriors with fierce eyes, with misshapen snouts resembling razors, appearing as if clad in silver armor;
some of them seem to be enjoying a sport in the waters of the sea through their constant emerging, diving, and darting about."
Supāraga said:
"These are neither humans nor non-humans;
they are indeed fish, so there is no need to fear them. However—"
"We have been drawn very far away even from the two cities;
this ocean is a garland of razors, so strive to turn back."
But because their ship was driven by a mass of water flowing with fierce velocity and by a westerly wind that carried it away to one side, those merchants were unable to turn back.
Then, as they gradually plunged in, beholding another ocean whose white waters were illuminated by the radiance of silver and made pale by masses of foam, they spoke to Supāraga with wonder:
"By what water is this great ocean possessed of such white silk-like [foam], as if submerged in its own froth?
Carrying forth, as it were, the liquid rays of the moon, it spreads on all sides like a smile. (AJm_14.14)
Supāraga said: "Alas!
One is indeed plunging into something exceedingly deep."
This ocean is known as the Ocean of Milk, and this one is the Ocean of Curds;
it is not possible to go further than this, so if you can, you must turn back.
The merchants said:
"Indeed, it is not even possible to delay the ship, much less turn it back, because of the extreme speed of the vessel and the adverse nature of the wind."

Then, having crossed even that ocean whose garland of moving waves was colored by the golden radiance [of the sun] and whose waters were tawny with flames of fire, those merchants, filled with wonder and curiosity upon beholding another ocean,
questioned Supāraga: "With its dark-blue waters rising up, anointed as if with the splendor of the morning sun..."
"Blazing like a great fire, what indeed is this, and from where has this great ocean come? (AJm 14.16)
Supāraga said:
"This ocean that appears here is renowned as Agnimālī.
It would indeed be most excellent if we were to turn back from this point."
Thus that Great-souled One spoke only of the name of that lord of rivers, for, being far-sighted, he did not mention the cause of the water's discoloration.

Then those merchants, having crossed even that ocean whose waters were illuminated by the luster of *puṣparāga* and *indranīla* gems, beheld another ocean whose color resembled the hue of ripe *kuśa* grass leaves; filled with curiosity, they asked Supāraga:
"Which ocean is this that shines forth, its waters having the color of ripe *kuśa* grass leaves?"
Like a flowering tree with its clusters of foam, it was variegated by the breaking of waves tossed by the force of the wind.
Supāraga said:
"O caravan leaders, let an effort be made to turn back;
indeed, it is no longer possible to proceed further than this."
This ocean, garlanded with *kuśa* grass, is like an elephant beyond control; forcibly carrying away its unbearable waters, it robs us of our delight.

Then those merchants, unable to turn the ship back even with the greatest effort, crossed that ocean as well and, beholding another sea whose waters were green with the mingled luster of bamboo-colored gems and lapis lazuli, asked Supāraga:
"With its waters possessing the emerald-green radiance of fresh meadows, it flows like the beauty of a new sward."
"Which ocean is this that is seen, adorned with foam as beautiful as white water-lilies?"
Then that Great Being, his heart burning with grief at the calamity that had befallen those merchants, heaved a long, hot sigh and spoke softly:
"We have come too far; it is painful for us to turn back.
This ocean is like the very edge of the world, like the Nala-flower garland."

Having heard that, those merchants, their minds overwhelmed by despair and the vigor of their limbs failing, sat right there, intent only on sighing. Even after crossing that ocean, at the time of evening, when the sun— with its orb of rays hanging low— was as if desirous of entering the ocean, [they saw] as if from the surging sea, or like falling thunderbolts...

They heard the tumultuous, exceedingly terrifying sound of the ocean, like the bursting of bamboo forests enveloped by fire— a sound that tears the ears and the heart. Upon hearing it, overcome by terror and with their minds trembling, they rose up suddenly and looked about in every direction.
They beheld that great mass of water falling like a precipice or a vast chasm; and seeing it, overwhelmed by supreme terror, they approached Supāraga and said:
"This sound of the lord of rivers is heard even from afar, as if splitting our ears and as if churning our hearts with fear, like that of one who is enraged."
As this entire body of water falls before us like a terrifying abyss, what is this ocean, and what do you consider to be the next course of action here?
Then that Great Being, filled with agitation, cried out, "Alas! Alas! and looking toward the ocean, said:
"That which, once reached, one does not return from, like the mouth of Death—its face turned away—that is this inauspicious Mare’s Mouth into which we have entered. (AJm 14.23)

Having heard that, those merchants—thinking, "We have come to the mouth of the mare"—abandoned all hope for life; their minds overwhelmed by the fear of death, some wept aloud, some lamented, and others cried out;
some, their senses bewildered by terror, did not know what to do.
In particular, some bowed down to the Lord of the Gods with minds impelled by distress;
others sought refuge with the Ādityas, Rudras, Aśvins, Maruts, and Vasus, while yet others fled to the ocean.
Some muttered various mantras, while others prostrated according to ritual before the Goddess;
some, approaching Supāraga, lamented piteously, performing various gestures of distress.
For you, who constantly dispel the fear of those fallen into calamity and are endowed with the virtue of compassion for others,
this is the time to employ that extraordinary power of yours.
O steadfast one, incline your heart to protect us who are afflicted, helpless, and have come to you for refuge;
for this ocean, out of anger, seeks to swallow us as if with the mouth of a mare.
"It is not right for you to neglect these people who are perishing in the midst of this flood of water;
the great ocean does not disregard your command, so let this lack of peace among them be restrained."
Then that Great-souled One, his heart tormented by intense compassion, spoke to those merchants as he composed himself:
"A certain remedial measure occurs to me even here;
I shall employ it, so for a moment, sirs, remain steadfast."
Then those merchants, their courage bolstered by the hope that "there is a remedy even for this," remained silent with their minds fixed intently upon it.

Then the Bodhisattva Supāraga, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and placed his right knee upon the ship, with all his being bowed in devotion, paid homage to the Tathāgatas and addressed those merchants:
"Listen, worthy merchants, and you distinguished deities who dwell in the ocean and the sky!"
As far back as I can remember my own self, and since the time I attained discernment,
I do not recall ever having intended to harm a living being anywhere.
By this word of truth and by the power of my merit,
may the ship turn back safely without reaching the Mare’s Mouth.

Then, by the power of that Great Being’s solemn resolve (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*) and by the splendor of his merit, the wind together with the force of the water turned back and caused the ship to return. Beholding the ship turned back, those merchants, their minds overflowing with supreme wonder and joy, announced to Supāraga with prostrations and respectful greetings: "The ship has returned! It has returned!"
Then that Great Being said to those merchants,
"May you all be steadfast;
let the cooling drinks be quickly brought up."

Thus instructed by him, those officials, their strength and energy aroused by joy, acted accordingly. Then that ship, situated upon the ocean, shone like a royal swan in a cloudless sky— resounding with the laughter of joyful people, its broad, white, cool, and beautiful wings spread wide.
When that ship, which had been moving with favorable currents and winds, proceeded at its own will with the ease of a celestial chariot,

Supāraga spoke to those merchants as the twilight— its cosmetic ointment of deep crimson— had faded, the canopy of darkness was being spread abroad, the quarters of the sky were becoming adorned with visible stars, and the path of the sun had begun its transition into the dominion of night with only a slight remnant of light remaining.
"O caravan leaders, let sand and stones be loaded onto the ship from the oceans you have seen, beginning with Nalamālin, as much as it can bear;
thus this vessel, though overwhelmed by the weight of the cargo, will not split its sides.
Furthermore, these sand and stones are considered auspicious and will certainly lead to the success of your gains."

Taking up from the places pointed out by deities whose minds were overcome with love and great respect for Supāraga, they loaded the ship with jewels such as lapis lazuli, mistaking them for sand and pebbles.
And in that very same single night, that ship arrived at Bharukaccha.
Then at dawn, their ships filled with silver, sapphire, beryl, and gold, arrived at the shore of their own country; with hearts overflowing with joy, they honored him with great affection.
Thus, even truthful speech based on righteousness dispels calamity, let alone its fruit; therefore, one should be a follower of righteousness.
In the description of relying upon spiritual friends as well, it should likewise be stated that those who rely upon spiritual friends attain what is beneficial.
The fourteenth is the Supāraga-jātaka.
15. The Matsya-jātaka:
"In this very world, the auspicious intentions of those possessed of virtuous conduct succeed, let alone in the next; therefore, one should strive for the purification of moral discipline."
Thus it is heard:

once, it is said, the Bodhisattva was the lord of the fish in a certain lake that was not very large, whose beautiful waters were adorned with white, red, and blue lotuses and water lilies; which was graced by pairs of swans, *kāraṇḍava* ducks, and ruddy geese; and whose shores were strewn with the blossoms of trees growing along its banks.
And because he had practiced the service of others for many previous births, even while remaining there [in that state], he was occupied with bringing about the welfare and happiness of others.
For through the power of habitual practice, both auspicious and inauspicious actions become second nature to men;
thus, such deeds are performed effortlessly in another birth, as if in a dream. (AJm 15.1)

With a heart fixed upon them as if they were his own beloved offspring, that Great Being bestowed the highest favor upon those fish through the sequence of giving, kind words, purposeful conduct, and so forth.
Restraining their mutual habit of harming one another and increasing their reciprocal affection,
he caused them to forget their nature as fish through the application of skillful means and his knowledge of expedients.
Thus, being properly protected by him, the multitude of fish attained supreme growth,
like a city freed from calamities by a king who acts with justice.
Then, at one time, due to the deficiency in the merit of sentient beings and the negligence of the sons of the gods appointed over the rains, the rain did not fall properly.
And because the rain fell improperly, that lake was not filled as before with fresh water as yellowish-white as the blossoms of the *kadamba* tree.
Gradually, as the summer season arrived, by the rays of the sun, which possessed exceedingly intense brilliance and seemed as if their movement were sluggish with exhaustion—
And that lake, being drunk up day after day by the earth scorched by its heat— as if by a wind accompanied by flames and longing for refreshment, as if out of thirst— became a mere puddle;
for the sun blazed during the summer season, and the sharp wind drew away the very flames.
The earth was not cool, as if afflicted by fever, and the waters seemed to dry up in anger.

Then the Bodhisattva, seeing the school of fish— which was being preyed upon even by flocks of crows, let alone by the flocks of birds wandering along the water's edge— overcome by despair and dejection, and reduced to mere gasping, was moved by compassion and fell into reflection: "Alas, what a grievous calamity has befallen these fish!"
Day by day the water diminishes as if competing with one's lifespan;
yet even now, the arrival of the rains is still perceived as being far off.
There is no means of retreat, nor who else could be our leader;
meanwhile, our enemies, rejoicing at our calamity, are closing in upon us.
Without a doubt, because this remainder of water is being exhausted,
they will be devoured by my enemies while I look on, even as they struggle.
Reflecting on what might be appropriate for this occasion, that Great Being saw a single resort for the distressed: the empowerment of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*).
His heart being oppressed by compassion, he sighed long and hot, looked up toward the sky, and said:
"I do not recall ever intentionally committing the taking of life, even when in the midst of supreme distress."
By this truth, may the King of the Gods cause the lakes to be filled with water and let it rain!

Then, through the power of that Great Being’s accumulation of merit, through the force of his resolve in truth, and through the influence of the gods, nāgas, and yakṣas whom he had propitiated, unseasonable clouds appeared on all sides. Their forms hung low with water, they resounded with deep and sweet thunder, and they were adorned with streaks of lightning. With their vast blue peaks, they seemed to be yawning or embracing one another with their outstretched arms of mountain summits.
Black clouds appeared,
as if measuring out the extent of the quarters and spreading darkness with their peaks;
reflected upon the mirror-like surface of the sky, the black clouds shone like the shadows of mountains.

Those masses of clouds shone forth, as if being praised by joyful peacocks with their closely joined cries and variegated dances; they were like wise men smiling gently amidst continuous, low rumbling.

Released as if by those very beings, streams of water fell like liberated [beings]; the dust was stilled, and a fragrant scent wafted unrestrainedly across the earth, scattered by the wind from the clouds.
Although intensified by contact with the summer heat, the power of the sun's rays vanished;
the waters, their mid-reaches agitated by rows of foam, flowed toward the lowlands.

Again and again, delighting the horizons with her rays of golden-yellow brilliance and receiving joy from the sound of the clouds as if they were musical instruments, the creeper-like lightning performed a dance, as it were.

Then, as the lake was being filled by pale streams of water flowing out from all sides, and as the flocks of birds, such as crows and others, scattered at the very moment the rain fell, while the shoals of fish were joyful having regained hope for life, the Bodhisattva— his heart drawn toward them with affection yet apprehensive that the rain might cease— addressed the rain-cloud again and again.
Thunder, O rain-cloud, with a deep and steady roar, driving away the crows' delight;
raining down waters that act as jewels, flashing with the brilliance of clinging lightning.
Having heard this, Śakra, the lord of the gods, his mind filled with supreme wonder, approached him in person and, seeking to please him, said:
"O Lord of Fishes, O one of great majesty, this is indeed the power of your own extraordinary truth;
for these clouds, with their lovely thundering, pour forth as if they were overturned jars."
This is indeed a great lapse of negligence on my part,
that I do not undertake the application of service for those like you, whose minds are set upon exertion for the sake of the world in their duties.
Do not harbor such anxiety beyond this point; for I am the one yoked to the burden of carrying out the duties of the virtuous.
Moreover, by relying upon your virtues, this land shall never again be subject to suffering in this way.
Having thus gratified him with such affectionate words, he vanished on the spot;
and that lake attained the highest abundance of water.

Thus, for those possessed of ethical discipline, even their virtuous intentions flourish in this very life, let alone in the next; therefore, one should strive for the purification of ethical discipline.
The fifteenth birth story, the Matsya-jātaka.
